📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside.
  • In a recent development, the crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck.
  • Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators notes Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

In a recent development, the crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

Industry observers note that according to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Sources indicate that charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly remarked which.

Industry observers note that mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

CHP indicates the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has mentioned a word about Autopilot.

Recent findings suggest that under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

The rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police remarked it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

Sources indicate that how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

In a recent development, two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

CHP hasn’t remarked whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing fresh rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

This is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

"what little effort went into the report"?

I disagree, a lot of effort went in to minimize the report, to portray it as an unremarkable accident.

That is the effort I find Tesla criminally responsible for.

It has been revealed that the CHP need the full report, no redactions. If they chose to censor it that is their task, not Tesla's.

It has been revealed that what stands out in this one is how little effort went into the report. Tesla knows the speed, knows the system was on, and has telematics. But it couldn’t fill in what the car hit, and it learned about three deaths in one of its cars from the news. Then it redacted the one field, the narrative, that would tell us what the car did.

In a recent development, tesla wants regulators and customers to trust FSD with no one watching. That trust has to be earned with data. A organization that seals the account of what its car did at 74 mph in a neighborhood, in a crash that killed three people, isn’t earning it.

Industry observers note that we’re asking CHP Placerville whether its investigators knew the system was engaged, whether they got Tesla’s raw data or Tesla’s summary of it, and what they found about the fire and the doors. If CHP never got the full data, how will it ever determine the cause?

F1 Driver Isack Hadjar Has a Very Specific 9-Minute Rule

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 22-year-old Red Bull Formula 1 driver has finally gotten his hands on Grand Theft Auto VI, and he's slightly concerned about what that might do to his free time.
  • Sources indicate that “It's going to ruin my life,” he jokes to Men's Health in the paddock ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix.
  • For now, at least, Hadjar has his priorities straight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ISACK HADJAR HAS a problem. The 22-year-old Red Bull Formula 1 driver has finally gotten his hands on Grand Theft Auto VI, and he's slightly concerned about what that might do to his free time.

Sources indicate that “It's going to ruin my life,” he jokes to Men's Health in the paddock ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix. He's only managed to squeeze in about 25 minutes of gameplay so far this weekend, but his verdict is already in: “It's amazing.”.

For now, at least, Hadjar has his priorities straight. “I'm a professional,” he states with a smirk. “When I know it's time to go to sleep, I go to sleep.”.

Industry observers note that that level of discipline extends well beyond bedtime. In a sport that demands lightning-fast reflexes, intense concentration, and serious physical endurance, Hadjar has developed a pretty specific routine to get his brain and body ready to perform.

Take his pre-race ritual, which he has down to a science. He stretches and warms up with his trainer, including juggling and reaction-time tests to prime the brain. He listens to rap music—French, American, or British—to get himself hyped.

Recent findings suggest that then, exactly nine minutes before the race begins, he starts putting in his earpieces. “Not 10, not 11, nine," he says.

According to recent reports, it's not a superstition or a lucky number. (That would be six, the number he drives with for Red Bull.) It’s simply what he’s found to be the perfect amount of time to get in the car and get ready to race. “I hate staying in the car doing nothing,” he says. “So for me, nine minutes is the maximum time.”.

While he enjoys the pre-race preparation, there's one part of training he'd happily skip: zone 2 cardio, running at a moderate pace to power up his endurance.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s just boring. I like conditioning more,” he notes. To get through it, he puts on a movie, TV show, or music. “It goes by quickly in the end, but it's just, I feel like it's a waste of time. But it's very important.”.

When the race is over, Hadjar's routine is considerably more relaxed. A good meal helps him switch his brain off—specifically, a burger with caramelized onions, cheddar, tomato, and lettuce. He’ll also watch anime and FaceTime his parents, especially after a good result.

And now, of course, there will be GTA VI waiting for him. Whether he'll be able to stick to that bedtime routine is another question.

Catch Hadjar in action this weekend at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, streaming live (and for free!) on Apple TV.

Sources indicate that hyundai appears to be testing a new high-tech setup in the IONIQ 5. A prototype was spotted with the door wide open, exposing a large display and a layout that looks very different from the current model.

Sources indicate that is the IONIQ 5 next in line for an overhaul? Another mysterious IONIQ 5 test mule was recently caught in a parking garage in South Korea, revealing what’s rumored to be Hyundai’s software-defined vehicle (SDV).

Hyundai is betting heavily on software, AI, autonomous driving, robotics, and more as it expands from a traditional auto manufacturer to a “software-centric mobility leader.”.

At the heart of it all is Hyundai Motor Group’s new Pleos Connect, an advanced in-vehicle infotainment and software platform.

Built on Android Automotive OS, Hyundai’s new setup features a larger, tablet-style infotainment screen with apps, split-screen views, and more. It’s similar to using a smartphone with an easier-to-use, customizable layout.

In a recent development, the Grandeur was the first to launch with Hyundai’s Pleos in Korea in May, followed by the IONIQ 3 in Europe. In the US, the fresh Tucson will be the first to go on sale with Pleos in early 2027.

Is the IONIQ 5 next in line? Hyundai aims to launch its first SDV as early as next year, and the IONIQ 5 appears to be a contender.

An IONIQ 5 test car was captured again (shown below) by @JHS_spyshot_official in a Korean parking garage, but this time the door was wide open, offering a clear view of the new setup.

A post shared by JHS (@jhs_spyshot_official).

Hyundai appeared to be testing automated parking features, and as you can see, the setup is considerably different from the current IONIQ 5.

A large infotainment display sits at the center that appears to be running Hyundai Pleos, instead of the current dual 12.3″ screens. Meanwhile, the steering wheel and dash both appear to be completely redesigned.

Although it’s hard to see, previous spy images show the IONIQ 5 SDV test car with no driver display, with all information expected to move to the large center infotainment screen.

By 2030, Hyundai Motor Group aims to equip around 20 million Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis vehicles with the new Pleos setup.

It has been revealed that guess I'm holding onto my 2023 EV6 for as long as I can. I saw a preview of the fresh software and think it looks pretty solid, but I am NOT a fan of the "huge tablet" dashboard.

My dad has a new Solterra and we took a long road trip in my EV6 last month. He noted my screens are so much more easy to see and use. The only issue I have is the top of the steering wheel obscures the icons at the top of my driver's screen, but I'd rather have that than a giant hulking tablet sitting in the middle of the dash.

The system is the “first tangible step” toward an SDV (Software-Defined Vehicle) architecture, Hyundai said, which will unlock upcoming in-car features, autonomous driving capabilities, and personalized driving experiences.

Over the summer, an IONIQ 6 prototype was spotted near Hyundai’s R&D hub in Europe with a similar high-tech setup.

With Hyundai planning to launch its first SDV as early as next year, we should learn more soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that there are many perks of being a Women’s Health style writer, and testing comfortable sneakers for work ranks very high on the list. My days are basically a rotation of steps—commutes, errands, long walks in the name of journalism—which means I’ve become extremely picky about what earns a spot on my feet. But time after time, I keep coming back to Hoka, aka the King of Cushion.

Since the brand introduced in 2009, Hoka has perfected the balance between support and comfort (the number one feature in a walking shoe), states podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM, foot surgeon and owner of Central Park Sole in Upcoming York City.

Hoka has not only asserted itself as a top contender in the sneaker scene, but the brand has also become a style statement, too, making ortho-looking shoes look cool with their plush cushioning. The brand churns out a bunch of styles for all sorts of activities, from running shoes to hiking boots, but Hoka’s walking shoes are some of my favorites. I get that combing through all the specs can get overwhelming, so luckily, I’ve done the legwork for you by testing and walking in Hoka sneaks for the past two years. Plus, I enlisted the help of Schaeffer and other WH editors to get the scoop on the right shoes for you.

Sources indicate that after testing nearly every Hoka model, the Clifton 11 reigns supreme for walking. I was also a fan of the previous Clifton 10, and the newest version feels very similar. It is by far the most comfortable model in the series to date, and it’s earned a spot in my shoe rotation for its supportive yet flexible cushioning that gives me a spring in my step.

According to recent reports, the first major difference I noticed is how light the Clifton 11 feels. Even after wearing it for several hours at a time, it doesn’t feel bulky or clunky. Which makes sense: Hoka did shave nearly half an ounce off the weight compared to the 10. The toe box is slightly more narrow, too, but I actually preferred the more secure fit because it kept my foot from sliding around without feeling cramped. If you like a little more wiggle room for your toes, I would suggest opting for the wide sizing, though.

According to recent reports, despite its lighter weight, it has an ample stack of foam padding throughout the midsole. That weightless yet cushiony feel makes it ideal for my longer walks throughout NYC. The shoe has a mild heel drop (the same as the previous model at 8 mm), which helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot.

I also found that the foam absorbed impact well on both pavement and the treadmill. My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never felt fatigued wearing this shoe. There's technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely notice it—instead, my stride just felt smooth and natural whether I was walking or running. I’m also a fan of the durable rubber outsole that gives plenty of traction. I never feel like I’m going to slip while wearing these, even when walking down slippery subway stairs.

Sources indicate that so far, the Clifton 11—which was debuted alongside the latest Clifton Pro— does a great job of keeping my feet comfy and supported. It’s a great shoe for anyone in need of a comfortable, everyday walking sneaker that can also handle the occasional jog (unlike the Clifton Pro, which is geared more toward high-speed running).

Read more: Hoka Clifton 11 and Clifton Pro Review.

According to recent reports, technically, the Mach 7 is a running shoe—but don’t let that marketing label fool you. The previous iteration, the Mach 6, took home our 2025 Fitness Award for top walking shoe thanks to its blend of responsive cushioning, breathability, and lightweight construction—and the Mach 7 has built on that winning formula with an updated outer and grippier bottom. I’ve walked more than 150 miles in the ultra-light, ridiculously comfortable sneaker, and not once have I felt even a bit of foot fatigue or soreness.

The midsole is stiff yet flexible, while the cushioning is relatively low-key compared to its popular sibling, the Bondi 9. But, its slimness is an illusion. In fact, it’s just as supportive as most Hoka models and still offers a spring-like sensation after your foot hits the ground for a comfortable stride. This style doesn’t offer any special stability features for people whose feet tend to roll while walking, but I found it still does a decent job of keeping my feet in a neutral position, despite my high arches and tendency to underpronate (or land on the outer edge of my feet).

In a recent development, I wear the standard size and haven’t had any challenges, but Accardi prefers the wide sizing, which she finds more suitable for her bunions and ability to spread her toes. If you have similar foot concerns or just like more wiggle room, we definitely recommend the wide fit.

While our one complaint with the Mach 6 was its lack of traction, I thankfully found that the Mach 7 features a more durable rubber at the heel and a stickier rubber up front, which makes a noticeable difference in grip.

According to recent reports, thanks to its incredible support and cushioning, the Gaviota 6 keeps my feet pain-free even after miles of wear. The shoe is designed with Hoka’s signature H-frame, which is a firm, dense foam in the midsole that provides a stable base to really lock your feet in place. I recently discovered that I have high arches, causing my ankles to roll inward when I walk, so this shoe has been a game-changer for me and my recent foot woes.

While the Gaviota 6 is geared toward flat arches on paper, I’m currently contending with a bit of foot fatigue from my new 1-mile-per-day (at least!) running goal, and the Gaviota 6 has given my dogs the TLC they need. That’s likely due to the combo of plush cushioning and stability tech. After weeks in the Gaviota 6, my gait naturally shifted from a heel strike to a midfoot strike—exactly what Schaeffer recommends for pain-free walking.

Other super supportive sneakers I’ve tried tend to have a stiff midsole. Not so with this shoe. It has a hefty EVA foam for a plush feel, like I’m walking on marshmallows. Plus, I found this foam also does a bang-up job of absorbing impact from my strides. In other words, it’s super easy on my joints. Bonus points: its fabric doesn’t rub at all, even when I’m wearing thin socks, which is a must-have when I’m clocking hundreds of miles in it.Weighing in at under nine ounces, the Gaviota 6 actually sheds half an ounce from the already lightweight Gaviota 5. I love that it feels lighter than it looks, but it still has a bulky look that may not vibe with everyone. FWIW, I love the chunky aesthetic and wear it with hiking gear, wide-leg trousers, and even casual dresses.

Plantar fasciitis (that painful inflammation under your arch) demands serious support, and the Hoka Bondi 9 delivers. It’s the brand’s plushest model, with cushioning that feels soft yet springy like you’re walking on clouds.

“I’ve been struggling with plantar fasciitis after months of half-marathon training, and this shoe—along with daily leg stretches—got me through long-haul walks pain-free,” states Accardi. That’s thanks to the Bondi’s plush underfoot cushioning and generous stack height. Schaeffer also recommends this shoe to his clients with plantar fasciitis, and says it provides a nice mix of cushion and stability. I also supinate and found that the Bondi 9’s premium foam midsole keeps my feet in a neutral position.

Industry observers note that contributor Lily Wohlner is also a mega-fan of this shoe. She's logged 15 miles walking in it and even wore it to the office to see how it holds up during long days on her feet. The verdict? It's the most comfortable shoe she owns, and she can wear it all day long without an ounce of foot pain.

In a recent development, compared to the last iteration, this pair looks less bulky and feels lighter, and our style team found that this streamlined aesthetic plays nicer with most casual fits. However, be aware the shoe runs a tad narrow. Ritchey says she doesn’t have particularly wide feet, but that the toe box is a bit too small. She walked over 17 miles in this shoe recently and started to blister slightly in her pinky toes.

Recent findings suggest that “The Arahi 8 has become my absolute companion running and walking shoe ever since I started bouncing back from my stress fracture,” Accardi indicates. “My podiatrist said I needed something firm and supportive—too much squish and flex could cause my feet to roll and exacerbate my injury—and the Arahi delivered.” Don’t let the sturdy midsole fool you: It’s relatively comfy for a stability shoe, with just enough give to keep things feeling smooth. Compared to the Arahi 7, this version hugs the foot better and offers noticeably more bounce-back with every step. It’s got that sweet spot of stability and responsiveness.

Fitness editor Cori Ritchey is a huge fan of the shoe’s “well-balanced cushioning,” saying that it feels plush underfoot but didn’t affect her stability while walking long distances or running. She loves that the toe box on the Arahi 8 is a bit wider than the Bondi 9, giving her plenty of room to spread her toes. But, if you are into plush, cloud-like cushioning, you may want to stick with the Bondi’s. The Arahi doesn’t have that marshmallow-like softness—it’s much firmer.

One of its standout features is the integrated H-frame support system: Strategically placed firmer foam that wraps around the sides of your foot to guide your stride and keep your foot in a neutral position. You can definitely feel the structure working, but the payoff in stability is huge, especially if you’re recovering, need extra support, or just want something you can rely on to keep your form in check.

As someone who never reties her shoe laces (I always slip my sneakers on), the Hoka Transport originally caught my eye with its toggle lace system that eliminates the hassle of tying and untying.

In a recent development, it reminds me of my favorite Salomon XT-6 shoes and has a cool granola-girl vibe—which makes sense, since it is technically a hiking shoe. However, I will admit that while the Transport 2 looks very similar to the original, I prefer the sleeker look of the previous iteration. This version is also slightly heavier, but it’s barely noticeable while walking, and I chalk it up to the slight increase in cushioning.

This shoe has quite a bit of cushion, but I found the midsole to be a bit on the stiffer side, meaning you just might want to plan for a longer break-in period before wearing it on long walks right off the bat. On the flip side, the firmness makes for a stable stride. It’s also great for neutral arches since it's not designed with any specific stability features in mind. But even with my slightly high arches, I felt locked in with every step.

Recent findings suggest that thanks to the high-traction, chunky outsole, I feel stable during trail walks across gravel, sandy paths, and uneven terrain. I also like that the outer shell material is Cordura, a water and abrasion-resistant mesh that’s built to prevent scuffs and withstand wear and tear.

Industry observers note that one thing to note: I went with the standard width, and the fit is a bit snug, especially with thicker socks. If you have wider feet, consider sizing up or opting for the wide version.

Hoka is known for its incredibly cushioned sneakers, but extreme cushioning is not always the best for keeping feet stable. In recent years, Hoka has leveled up their offering with more stability options, but the right pick depends on how your foot moves. If your stride is balanced, go for a neutral shoe like the Clifton or Bondi. These models provide cushioning and support without changing your natural gait.

It has been revealed that if your foot tends to roll inward (aka overpronation) or outwards (supination), a stability Hoka shoe like the Arahi or Gaviota features extra structure along the arch and heel to keep your feet aligned and locked in. This lowers your risk of aches and injury.

A popular Hoka sneaker, like the Bondi or Clifton, has super-thick cushioning made of EVA foam that is rubber-like and incredibly durable. With each step, it compresses and provides a snappy bounce. Despite the Hokas’ bulky look, they’re all relatively lightweight at under 10 ounces—hefty enough to keep your foot locked in, but light enough not to bog you down. Plus, several Hoka styles feature a "rocker bottom," which refers to a little lift under the heel and toe so those two parts of the shoe don’t touch the ground when standing still, similar to the base of a rocking chair. That shape helps you to walk from heel to toe, which means you exert less energy to propel your strides.

It has been revealed that some Hoka sneakers are designed for specific arch types: flat, neutral, and high. For example, the Gaviota is designed with flat feet in mind; the Clifton is designed for neutral arches; and the Bondi is suitable for high arches. If you’re unsure of your arch type, a simple test is to dip your foot into water and step onto a piece of paper. If you see your entire foot, it’s flat, while seeing half means it’s neutral. Seeing barely anything means you have a high arch.

A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer claims to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

It has been revealed that with their cloud-like cushioning, springy soles, and ample support, Hoka sneakers absorb impact from every step and keep feet locked in a neutral position. That makes them ideal for hot girl walks, a 12-3-30 walking workout, and taking your pup for a leisurely stroll.

It has been revealed that topping the list is the Hoka Clifton 11. I love the super supportive, plush midsole that keeps my feet from rolling and feels ultra-flexible. A close second is the Hoka Mach 7, our runner-up that’s technically a running shoe but totally crushes it for walking, too. It’s light, bouncy, and built for those who like to switch up their stride.

Sources indicate that over the past two years, I’ve been testing Hoka sneakers alongside my team for a comprehensive approach to the best walking shoes for every foot type and stride. Women’s Health editors have been testing Hoka sneakers since the brand launched in 2009. For this enhancement, I tested the updated models alongside WH fitness editor Cori Ritchey and fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi. Along with Schaeffer’s insights, I evaluated each for its cushioning, stability, and arch type.

The 10 Best Walking Shoes for Men, According to Men’s Health Editors

📅 30 Aug 2019 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that WALKING IS A great way to keep a steady exercise routine, even when you're not in the mood for more intense workouts.
  • "All [walking] shoes should feel snug around your foot, have good arch support, the heel shouldn’t slip around, and there should be adequate room in the toe box," recommends Mark J.
  • It has been revealed that since walking shoes can wear down quickly with everyday use, having one (or two) solid pairs in rotation is a smart move.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that WALKING IS A great way to keep a steady exercise routine, even when you're not in the mood for more intense workouts. Engaging in walking not only provides a gentle form of physical activity, but can also promote post-workout recovery and overall blood circulation. What can motivate you to get out for a few extra weekly walks? A pair of ultra-comfortable walking shoes that keep your feet happy long after you've reached your target.

"All [walking] shoes should feel snug around your foot, have good arch support, the heel shouldn’t slip around, and there should be adequate room in the toe box," recommends Mark J. Mendeszoon, DPM, a board-certified podiatrist and foot and ankle surgeon.

It has been revealed that since walking shoes can wear down quickly with everyday use, having one (or two) solid pairs in rotation is a smart move. Below, we’ve rounded up the best men’s walking shoes of the year—tested, podiatrist-reviewed, and chosen for comfort, support, and all-day wearability.

Industry observers note that one crucial lesson we've learned from Mendeszoon is not to focus only on shoe length when determining your ideal fit. According to him, it's equally essential to consider shoe width—much like with running shoes. Many brands now offer a range of widths, so understanding your foot anatomy is key to the right fit. "Wear the same socks you wear when you walk when trying them on and remember that our feet expand while walking.".

Once you find the right pair, keep in mind to replace them after you've racked up some miles. "It is important to realize that shoes are generally good for 500 to 600 miles," notes Mendeszoon. Even when you're primarily sporting them for walking. Ready to step into action? Then check out our guide to the best walking shoes for men below.

The Hoka Clifton 11 continues the franchise's tradition of plush comfort and podiatrist-approved design—earning another nod from the American Podiatric Medical Association. This version builds on what made the Clifton 9 and 10 favorites by refining the jacquard knit upper for a more adaptive fit, while still delivering the high-stack CMEVA foam that gives each stride a cloud-like feel.

The Clifton remains one of the lightest max-cushion shoes in its class; this version is even a little lighter than the 10. Its signature Smooth Metarocker geometry helps roll you forward with less effort, ideal for long walks, recovery days, or standing for hours. While it's technically a running shoe, walkers and all-day wearers have gravitated toward the Clifton for its smooth ride and day-to-night versatility.

Recent findings suggest that I personally have had a lot of friends who love the Hoka Clifton 11 and are on their feet all day working in retail and hospitals. If you liked the 9 and 10, the 11 stays true to the formula—with subtle tweaks that make it feel just a little softer, a little smoother, and still seriously easy on the feet.

Read More: Best Hoka Shoes for Walking.

If your walking routine takes you through city streets, sidewalks, or even the gym, the On Cloud X4 is built to keep pace with style. This newest version of On’s beloved crossover trainer retains its signature featherweight feel but adds key comfort upgrades that make it better suited for all-day wear. The breathable mesh upper stays cool and flexible, while plusher materials around the heel and tongue provide a more dialed-in, cushioned fit than the X3.

Industry observers note that the real enhancement lies in the underfoot tech: the Hellion superfoam midsole delivers soft landings, and the X-shaped Speedboard adds forefoot flex and energy return, whether you're walking forward or moving side to side. A midfoot cage adds extra structure, while a grippy rubber outsole gives you confident traction on pavement or polished floors.

This is still a firmer-feeling shoe, so don’t expect the plushness of a max-cushion trainer, but the Cloudtec pods adapt nicely to your stride and deliver a responsive feel that’s great for quick city walks or active errands.

This newest version of the Glycerin, the Glycerin 22, leans into what the series does best: plush comfort and a dialed-in neutral fit. The nitrogen-infused midsole foam has been fine-tuned for even better softness and smoother transitions, making it ideal for long walks when comfort is a top priority.

Unlike traditional stability shoes, the Glycerin 22 doesn’t use any rigid support posts. Instead, it relies on a wider platform and balanced midfoot geometry to provide a naturally stable base without feeling corrective. The result is a super-soft, highly neutral ride that feels consistent from heel strike to toe-off, whether you have 2 miles or 12 miles ahead of you.

In a recent development, the upper remains breathable and accommodating, and the shoe's durable outsole is built to handle high weekly mileage without wearing down quickly. It’s not flashy, but it’s reliable, and that’s exactly why people keep coming back to it.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for a reliable walking shoe that won’t wreck your budget, the Asics Gel-Pulse 17 builds on the success of the 15 with a few key upgrades to comfort and breathability. The FF BLAST midsole and signature GEL cushioning are still here. Meaning you get a soft, responsive ride whether you’re walking city blocks or putting in time on the treadmill. What’s new is the jacquard mesh upper, which offers a lighter, more ventilated feel than last year’s engineered mesh. It helps your feet breathe better on warm days or longer walks without compromising the structure you need for all-day support.

One standout design feature is the elevated midsole through the center, which enhances support and impact absorption across key pressure points. While the foam leans on the firmer side, the added GEL insert softens landings, making it a strong pick for steady-paced daily walks. Stability gets a boost too—thanks to strategic bumpers along the heel that cradle the foot, paired with a rigid heel counter that helps limit excess movement.

If you liked the 16, this one feels like a natural upgrade—just a bit cooler and more dialed in for summer.

The Kuru Atom 2 is designed as a comfort-focused athletic shoe that blends performance features with orthopedic support, making it also one of the best latest shoes for stability on the market. The minimalistic style behind the shoe appeals to me, especially when opting for the white or black colorways. I’ll also say that I was impressed at how easily the shoe slipped on, which is a bit of a non-negotiable for me unless I’m doing a trail run or putting in a lot of miles.

According to recent reports, the first thing I noticed was how comfortable the shoe was, with its cushioned midsole and KURUSOLE heel shock absorption still providing a solidly responsive ride. This makes it a perfect pick for anyone looking for a daily trainer for low mileage or full days of walking. The Atom 2 offers a moderate improvement over the shoe’s previous energy return, but it still isn’t a running shoe you want to hit the pavement with for long distances.

Industry observers note that the Kuru Atom 2 is a little heavy on the foot, which comes from the stability and durability that it provides. And thanks to the clean aesthetic, it fits in almost any setting, from the track to the grocery store.

The Brooks Ghost 17 proves why this Seattle-based brand remains a household name in performance footwear. Founded in 1914, Brooks has built its reputation on reliability, comfort, and a no-frills design approach—and the Ghost line is the perfect example of that. While the brand has recently taken steps to modernize its look and appeal to a younger generation, the Ghost 17 still leans traditional in the best way: It’s well-cushioned, durable, and consistent from mile one to mile 100.

The Brooks Ghost has long been a go-to for runners and walkers alike—and the Ghost 17 kept that reputation alive with subtle but smart upgrades. This version uses an air mesh upper for breathability, along with a redesigned kickback collar that cradles the heel without rubbing or slipping. The biggest change from the Ghost 16, though, is underfoot: Brooks added nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam in the heel and forefoot, giving the shoe a softer, more cushioned feel than previous versions. We should note that the Ghost 18 just released, and while we’re still in the early stages of testing it, it still uses that DNA Loft v3 foam but gets a fully rebuilt upper and tongue.

What makes the Ghost 17 such a standout is its adaptability. Whether you're on your feet for hours, squeezing in a quick power walk, or just want something that holds up across daily mileage, this is an easy choice. It’s not flashy—but that’s kind of the point. It’s durable, balanced, and built for comfort, making it an ideal “one-shoe-fits-most” option. And with the Ghost 18 just releasing, the price drop on the 17 still makes it worthwhile.

Read More: Best Moisture-Wicking Socks.

In a recent development, asics has refined the Gel-Nimbus line year after year, and the twenty-eighth iteration is one of its most luxurious yet. Known for max cushioning and long-wear comfort, this model upgrades the upper with a premium, breathable knit that feels as good as it performs. The toe box is also more spacious than in previous versions. A welcome relief for walkers who often feel squeezed in standard neutral shoes.

Recent findings suggest that underfoot, the Gel-Nimbus 28 still delivers a soft and stable ride, thanks to its combo of lightweight foam and added gel (FF Blast Plus ECO) cushioning in the forefoot and heel. The 8mm drop subtly rolls the foot forward, creating that ideal balance between protection and propulsion. The flexible knit tongue and solid heel lockdown add to the premium feel, making it a go-to for long walks, recovery days, or even light runs.

Men's Health Deputy Editor Paul Kita enjoyed how they felt structured, but not restrictive. Plus, Asics beefed up the outsole for better traction and longer wear. This pair will keep pace with more use. And while it's built for a neutral gait, it plays nicely with custom insoles if you need more arch support or pronation control.

In a recent development, two defining features set Altra shoes apart: a roomy toe box and a zero-drop platform. This combination ensures an anatomic fit and promotes a natural gait. Your feet enjoy greater freedom to move naturally, allowing your toes to flex and bend as you walk, which encourages better biomechanics and can reduce strain on your foot's structures.

Compared to other Altras, the Via Olympus 2 leans more toward plush than performance. The wide-base footbed adds stability, while the rocker-shaped sole still promotes a smooth forward roll with each step—even if it’s more subtle during walking than running. That extra room in the toe box and midfoot also comes in handy during longer efforts, giving your foot space to swell without feeling cramped.

In a recent development, "I love super high stack shoes like this, and Altra’s dedication to extra-roomy toe boxes makes the Via Olympus 2 even more comfortable," notes Williams. "The rocker shape is less pronounced on my walks than when I run in them, but it’s still noticeable for turnover on each step.".

If you're planning long walks, you'll appreciate how the shoe's roomy toe box accommodates the natural expansion that occurs during extended physical activity.

Read More: Best Wide Toebox Shoes.

Fashion meets function with this shoe. It showcases a stylish design while seamlessly integrating waterproof features, exceptional durability, and a rocker bottom that ensures a buttery-smooth walking experience. It not only performs well, but looks good doing it.

According to recent reports, it's explicitly designed for outdoor activities, making it an ideal choice for those who do most of their walking in nature. Thanks to its waterproof properties, my feet stay snug and dry, even in challenging weather conditions. Whether I'm trudging through rain-soaked paths or navigating puddles, these shoes provide unwavering protection for my feet.

According to recent reports, let's talk about Keen's newly patented "constant curve" construction. This design is engineered to encourage forward momentum in the wearer's stride, similar to most Hoka models. The rocker bottom facilitates a smooth transition from heel strike to toe-off, which Keen hopes can make walking more enjoyable for wearers. Based on my personal experience with these shoes, I'd say Keen has succeeded. I find myself walking faster and expending less effort, especially during long or uphill treks.

Although some reviewers have noted a rubbery off-gassing scent when the shoes are fresh out of the box, I didn't find it particularly noticeable (and I'm pretty sensitive to smells).

Read More: Best Treadmill Running Shoes.

Sources indicate that the Kuru Atom Trail is a purpose-built trail walking shoe designed to protect your heels, support your stride, and keep you moving confidently over rough ground. Its standout feature is the brand’s proprietary Kuru Sole, a dynamic midsole system that flexes with each step to cup and cradle the heel. Compared to traditional heel cradles, this one offers more adaptability and a locked-in feel. This is especially helpful for walkers who deal with heel pain or plantar fasciitis.

On the trail, the Atom Trail holds its own. A synthetic upper with rugged TPU overlays adds structure and durability, while the gusseted tongue helps block out debris. The outsole is aggressive and grippy, built for varied surfaces. It’s not the lightest or most responsive option out there. Which is why we wouldn’t recommend it for trail running but rather for long hikes, uneven terrain, and daily dog walks on gravel or dirt paths; it’s an excellent pick.

Sources indicate that mendeszoon puts it best: "This is a true traditional trail shoe that provides great support, comfort, and protection against the elements and uneven and challenging terrain." Our only qualm is that it's a little heavy and not particularly responsive, which is why we wouldn't recommend running it. But it excels in what it's meant for—trail walking.

Bonus points: it’s made with fully vegan materials and has enough breathability to handle summer hikes without overheating your feet.

Read More: Best Trail Running Shoes.

Sources indicate that look for walking shoes with support and stability features labeled for your specific foot type. "Consider your foot type and [walking] gait," says Dr. Bradley Schaeffer, DPM. "The goal is to keep your lower body in alignment as much as possible." Features such as a firm heel counter, a supportive midsole, and a secure lacing system can provide the stability you need for comfortable walking and to keep your feet properly aligned.

It has been revealed that when it comes to classification, if the shoe is stable, it is designed to help offset pronation, which is the inward rolling of the feet after landing on the ground. When a shoe is neutral, it lacks the stabilizing features, allowing your foot to fall more naturally. When a shoe is moderate, it is somewhere between those two worlds.

"Cushioning absorbs shock and helps to avoid tissue irritation and damage," explains Schaeffer. It's key to choose walking shoes with sufficient cushioning to absorb impact and shock with each step. Look for shoes with cushioned insoles and midsoles made from materials like foam or gel to ensure a comfortable walking experience, especially for longer walks or on hard surfaces.

Industry observers note that decide if you prefer soft cushioning for impact absorption and comfort or a more responsive feel. Some shoes offer a balance between the two, so choose based on your preferences and walking style.

Sources indicate that if you're in the market for a walking shoe to take you long distances frequently, be sure the models you're considering are relatively lightweight. Unless we're talking about a stability or trail shoe, which feature additional materials for added durability and support, that means under 11 ounces.

Pay attention to the upper material of the walking shoes, as it can impact comfort, breathability, and durability. Opt for shoes with breathable and flexible uppers made from materials like mesh or knit fabric to help keep your feet cool and comfortable. Additionally, keep an eye out for features like padded collars and tongues for even more comfort and support.

I’m a certified strength and conditioning specialist based in Fresh York and a fitness writer who loves trying the latest gear and raving to my loved ones about his latest discoveries. I have a dog, and I take him for walks twice a day. I also trek through the city from Queens to Manhattan five to six times per week. I have a pretty full roster of clients that I see in-person for training sessions and hit about 15,000 to 20,000 steps per day. Needless to say, I am on my feet A LOT, so I need to be on top of my game when it comes to comfy footwear.

Recent findings suggest that I also got some assistance from Men’s Health fitness editors and medical advisors. We spent months of testing and researching to create this guide. Over the past few years, we’ve logged miles in more than 40 pairs of walking and running shoes from top brands like Asics, Hoka, Brooks, On, and more. Led by Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM and Fitness Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, along with expert input from podiatrists Schaeffer and Mendeszoon, we evaluated each shoe for fit, comfort, cushioning, support, durability, and value. We also considered real-world feedback from testers who wore these shoes during daily walks, commutes, and all-day wear.

From minimalist trainers to max-cushioned picks, we curated this list to meet a variety of foot types, walking styles, and comfort preferences—so you can find the pair that’s right for your stride.

Understanding your foot type is essential for finding the right walking shoes that offer optimal comfort and support. There are three primary arch types based on arch height: neutral, high, and flat. To determine your arch type, you can start with a simple "wet test," Mendeszoon recommends. Wet your feet and stand on a surface like concrete, sand, or a flattened paper bag. Examine the imprint left by your foot.

According to recent reports, if your foot leaves a complete, flat imprint, you likely have low arches and would benefit from arch support or stability shoes. If the imprint indicates the heel, outer side of the foot, ball of the foot, and toes, but not the arch, you might have a neutral or high arch.

While the wet test provides a basic idea, factors such as weight, biomechanics, and overall fitness also help determine your arch type accurately. For a more detailed analysis, consider visiting a local chiropractic clinic, podiatry practice, or high-quality running shoe store. Some locations offer foot scans that provide intricate information about your feet and arches.

Sources indicate that todd Sinett from Tru Whole Care in New York highlights a special machine called the Foot Levelers Digital Foot Scanner, which identifies specific pressure points on your feet that could be linked to back pain. This advanced tool offers precise measurements for customized orthotics, ensuring tailored support for your unique foot structure.

Yes, running shoes can absolutely be worn for walking, according to Mendeszoon. In fact, they may offer some added benefit compared to conventional walking shoes.

Running shoes are designed to absorb the impact of running, which means they can also provide good shock absorption when walking. Many people choose to wear running shoes for walking because of added support and flexibility, too.

Industry observers note that one downside: Running shoes tend to be heavier and less breathable than walking shoes because of their more durable design. So, it's important to note that they may not be the best choice for long-distance walking.

Industry observers note that it's vital to replace your walking shoes regularly to ensure adequate support and cushioning, probably more frequently than you think. As a general rule of thumb, it's recommended to replace walking shoes every 300 to 500 miles (or every 3 to 5 months for those who walk for at least 45 minutes at least 3 times per week).

Recent findings suggest that the specific lifespan of a shoe depends on several factors, including the frequency and intensity of use, the shoe's quality, and the type of surface you typically walk on. There are a few signs to look out for that may indicate it's time to replace your shoes:.

Ultimately, it's notable to listen to your body and pay attention to any signs of discomfort or pain when walking. If you notice any of the above signs, it's a good idea to start looking for a newly introduced pair of walking shoes.

It has been revealed that powerlifting legend Mark Bell is a huge fan of walking for weight loss, as is Will Smith. This guy lost 60 pounds with walking and bodyweight workouts. And this guy lost 200 pounds by walking and eating a CICO diet. It's all about starting to add to your daily step count, and really sticking with it.

It has been revealed that "Starting slow and working your way up is better than overdoing it and giving up," Chris Gagliardi, a certified personal trainer at the American Council on Exercise, previously told Men's Health. An easy way to approach it: Commit to a quick 10-minute walk after dinner, and gradually increase the duration as you become more comfortable with daily movement.

Step counting also helps. "If you’re only getting 3,000 steps on a typical day, don’t try to get 10,000 steps the next day. That can be really discouraging. Aim for 5,000 every day for a week. Then go up to 7,000 the next week," walking coach Michele Stanten, founder of MyWalkingCoach.com and author of The Walking Solution, previously told Men's Health.

As a longtime distance runner, my feet can get pretty roughed up after a grueling workout—even with the proper running shoes. But since I don’t have the time or endless funds to regularly hoof it to my local spa for a foot massage or pedicure, a home foot bath is my go-to. The best foot baths allow you to soak your tired toes, with extra features like bubbles, jets, and massage functions to help your feet feel rejuvenated.

In a recent development, A good foot soak at the end of a long day or workout can do wonders for your mental health, too, ultimately supporting your overall health. But unsurprisingly, a lot of the potential perks from home foot baths revolve around your feet. These baths can help boost circulation in your feet and combat inflammation that could lead to pain, swelling, and overuse injuries if it’s left unchecked, indicates Bradley Schaeffer, DPM, a podiatrist and foot surgeon specializing in sports medicine in Latest York City. Plus, now that we’re at peak cozy season, shopping for a great foot bath for yourself or a loved one (it’s a great gift for her!) is a cost-effective way to give your feet some R&R.

Doing foot baths a few times a week can help to slough off dead skin that builds up quickly, leaving you with softer, less grody-looking feet, says Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois.

Not all foot baths are created equal, and it’s important to choose one based on your needs. So, if bubbles make you feel uncomfortable (me, hi), a foot bath that simply swirls around warm water may be more your speed. We also tapped Schaeffer, Lockwood, and Suzanne C. Fuchs, DPM, a podiatrist at Luxe Podiatry in Jupiter, Florida, for their advice on what to look for when shopping for these foot health-supportive devices and to get their feedback on their favorites.

Sources indicate that using that guidance and our personal experience, we found factors like size, weight, and additional features matter when choosing a foot bath. At baseline, a foot bath is a container to hold water to soothe your feet. But there are plenty of specific features to keep in mind when shopping for a foot bath.

In a recent development, the Hospan Collapsible Foot Spa packs a lot of features into a device you can fold flat. A huge highlight is the eight groups of massaging balls that go to work to ease pressure on the bottoms of your feet. (These aren’t motorized, but you can run your feet over them for a soothing effect.) While it’s a good idea to start out with warm or hot water, the Hospan Collapsible Foot Spa has temperature adjustment, allowing you to ramp up the heat between 95 and 118 degrees Fahrenheit without having to toss in more liquid. An LED display keeps tabs on the water temperature, giving you real-time information on how hot it is.

Industry observers note that as the name suggests, this foot bath is collapsible and drops down when it’s not in use, making it easy to slide into or under tight spaces. A few potential downsides to consider: Hospan’s bubbles aren’t the strongest you’ll find, and this is a pricier bath when it’s not on sale, although it’s usually marked down a few times a year. But if you’re looking to pamper your feet with a range of options and are okay with investing a little extra, this is a solid choice that will hold up well and does just about everything.

Read More: Best Stress Relief Gifts.

It’s hard to find a foot bath that checks all the boxes, but the Conair Soothing Pedicure Foot Spa Bath comes really close. This bath allows you to get a good soak with a few extras to take your experience to a newly introduced level. “This model features massage settings, which can enhance relaxation,” Fuchs says.

According to recent reports, this bath has a modest price tag of $30, which is significantly less than some others you’ll come across. It also uses vibration for a massage and has a pinpoint massage tool in the center in case you want to work on a particular area of your foot. While there’s no bubble feature, not everyone is into bubbles (they tickle my feet, which isn’t my favorite).

Conair’s foot bath is easy to use and clean, and offers plenty of opportunities to pamper your feet. The Conair Soothing Pedicure Foot Spa Bath uses a toe-touch control to turn the vibration settings on and off, although there’s no remote. This bath isn’t powerful enough to heat up cool or room temperature water, but it does a solid job of keeping already-warm liquid at the same temperature.

Not every foot bath has a bubble feature, and some are stronger than others. If bubbles are a priority for you, Fuchs recommends the Homedics Smart Space Elite Foot Bath. “Known for its bubbling action, this foot spa provides a soothing experience,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that the bath delivers plenty of bubbles, along with heat, to create a spa-like feel while you soak. It also has three pedicure attachments that pop into the center: a massager, brush, and pumice stone. Those attachments neatly fit into on-board storage when they’re not being used. An ergonomic footbed with massaging bristles on the bottom of the bath also helps cushion your soles while you rest. The whole thing folds up pretty small, and has a special locking system for when it’s filled up.

According to recent reports, if you’re interested in a foot bath that will give you a shiatsu-type massage, this isn’t it. But if you love the idea of blissfully scrolling on your phone while your feet are surrounded by warm, bubbly goodness, the Homedics Smart Space Elite Foot Bath is the right choice.

Read More: Best Acupressure Mats.

According to recent reports, getting the temperature just right in your foot bath can be tricky. But the Sharper Image Spa Haven Foot Bath has temperature control, allowing you to punch in the level of heat you want up to 108 degrees and let it go to work for you. This foot bath is loaded with features, including separate bubble and heat options, and free-spinning massaging rollers on the bottom that allow you to control the pressure and speed. (The rollers are removable for cleaning.).

The bubbling action is delivered in your choice of four speeds, and there’s also a removable pumice stone to help get rid of calluses and dead skin. When you’re done with your foot bath, just open the drain plug to let the water seep out. The only major downside to this foot bath (besides the high price) is that it’s not collapsible. But that also means it’s sturdy enough to rest your feet on the side when you want to take a break—a feature you won’t find in baths that break down.

Sources indicate that the Medical King Foot Spa has six sets of massaging rollers to help knead out stress and pain after a long day. Couple that with bubble jets, vibration settings, and a built-in heater, and you’ve got a recipe for a good time.

This relatively affordable foot bath comes with a remote control that doubles as a control panel, with clear buttons to adjust the massage mode and flip through three temperature settings as you kick back. You can also set a timer to cut off the features whenever you want. The foot bath is collapsible, so storage under your bed or couch shouldn’t be an problem. This foot bath delivers if you’re looking for a way to work out kinks in your soles without having to put in any major effort.

Read More: Best Compression Boots.

Industry observers note that you can splash out on a bunch of different features when it comes to a foot bath, but sometimes you just want a standard soak. If that’s the case—and you want to save some cash, too—consider the Mantello Foot Bath. This barebones bath is as basic as they come, but it has a few features that elevate it above your standard plastic bucket.

The bath has a sturdy plastic design that won’t tip over easily. It’s also deep, giving you plenty of space to soak your calves, too. The base has built-in arch support and raised dots for a little something extra while your feet relax. The open design means it’s easy to clean, too. There are no bubbles, massagers, or built-in heaters. But for a mere $23, what do you expect? If you’re just looking to unwind with a solid soak, this is a great choice.

In a recent development, “Foot baths can offer several benefits for foot health,” Fuchs notes. She lists off a bunch of potential perks, including helping your muscles (and mind) relax, improved circulation, removing the buildup of dirt and bacteria, soothing conditions like athlete’s foot or plantar fasciitis, and exfoliation. Of course, you don’t have to use a foot bath to have good foot health—but many people find that it can be a comfortable way to support it.

Should you use Epsom salts in your foot bath?

In case you’re not familiar with them, Epsom salts can help soften skin and support muscle relaxation. Fuchs recommends adding Epsom salts or essential oils to your tub to ramp up the relaxation and health perks.

The odds are good that you’ll be hauling a foot bath in and out of a storage spot on a regular basis. Most foot baths aren’t overly heavy, but some higher-tech options have more heft to them than others. (The baths we recommend range from 1 pound to 9 pounds.) Just take a peek at the weight to make sure you can comfortably carry your device around.

If your feet are on the larger side, you want to make sure there’s enough room for them to fit comfortably inside your bath. Also, that foot bath has to go somewhere, both when it’s put away and in use. Check the dimensions and compare them to where you plan to use your bath, along with the drawer or closet space where you plan to stash it, to make sure you have enough room.

In a recent development, this came up with every podiatrist we spoke to. “Feet can get gross and we want to be able to have a sanitized bath each time we use it,” Lockwood indicates. Schaeffer agrees. “Bacteria can grow in these, raising the risk of infections,” he points out. With that, it’s crucial to look for a foot bath that’s easy to clean. That usually means the bath can be disassembled for scrub-downs or at least have very detailed cleaning instructions.

This isn’t a requirement, but having the option to collapse your foot bath can be helpful if you’re short on storage space. Many collapsible foot baths can fold down relatively flat, and have locking mechanisms to keep them in place when they’re in use. But if you have the room, you might prefer the sturdier design of a non-collapsible foot bath.

Sources indicate that many foot baths have features to give you more than a good soak, like bubbles, jets, and massagers. Some will heat up the water for you, and others have helpful elements like remote control, rollers, and pumice stones. These extra features usually come with a higher price, so consider what you will and won’t use if you’re looking to save on a bath.

Sources indicate that to choose the best foot baths, I first relied on my own personal experience with these tools, making sure to weed out options I’ve used that have leaked, broken, or just not lived up to the hype. From there, I reached out to three podiatrists located across the country for their feedback on what to look for while shopping for these baths. I also utilized in-house testing by Women’s Health editors for units we got feet into. Each foot bath was evaluated on size, weight, ease of cleaning, and extra features like bubbles and built-in massagers to create the final list. Keeping all of that in mind, these foot baths are worth snapping up to get your soak on.

Tesla confirms €3B Cybercab factory at Giga Berlin for up to 1M a year

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany.
  • Recent findings suggest that that’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one.
  • Plant manager André Thierig revealed the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany. The company confirmed today a first €3 billion investment in a fresh production building at Giga Berlin designed for up to 1 million Cybercabs a year, with production planned for 2029.

Recent findings suggest that that’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.

Plant manager André Thierig revealed the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.

Industry observers note that if you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we announced a first investment of around € 3b in a fresh manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW.

Per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the new production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla intends to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The firm says it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”.

Recent findings suggest that it leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the upcoming hall will be bigger than the original factory.

Recent findings suggest that the building isn’t latest. Tesla laid out a proposal to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only noted the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

Recent findings suggest that giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

So the upcoming hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

It has been revealed that the EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

In a recent development, tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

Rules can move in three years. The Commission has remarked it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

Tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

Tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

Industry observers note that the Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU mentioned no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

And the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

That’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

This is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

Recent findings suggest that good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

Sources indicate that will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.
