  • It has been revealed that THE WORLD OF elite running moves fast.
  • Industry observers note that the Swoosh’s last pinnacle racer, the Alphafly 3, was unveiled all the way back in November 2023 (the late Kelvin Kiptum broke the marathon world record wearing a prototype of the model at the Chicago Marathon earlier that year).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that THE WORLD OF elite running moves fast. That might seem an obvious observation, sure—but it applies beyond the athletes chasing finish lines to the gear they use for peak performance. So as world records fell and mass race participation swelled over the last few years, hardcore running shoe lovers wondered: Where is Nike, and what’s taking so long to unleash the brand’s next top-level super shoe?

Industry observers note that the Swoosh’s last pinnacle racer, the Alphafly 3, was unveiled all the way back in November 2023 (the late Kelvin Kiptum broke the marathon world record wearing a prototype of the model at the Chicago Marathon earlier that year). While the shoe has been a massively popular race day pick for all kinds of runners from 2024 on, other brands entered the super shoe space Nike originated and put out light, fast racers that offered speedier specs and took podium places (including a fresh marathon world record, the first sub-2-hour finish that bested even Eliud Kipchoge’s 2019 exhibition run in an earlier Alphafly model). Nike put out some great releases in the interim, including the excellent Vomero Plus and Premium models—but the top echelon of the racing line remained untouched.

After a nearly three-year gap, the Alphafly 4 is here. I got my feet in a pair ahead of its October 29 launch and my fall race, the NYC Marathon, so I put the super shoe to the test on the city’s streets for 26.2 miles (and a few more along the training cycle) to see if it lives up to the Alphafly name.

THE ALPHAFLY 4 builds on the same design language as its predecessor, with two of Nike’s signature Air Zoom units in the forefoot, a high stack of ZoomX foam, and a carbon fiber plate. But there are new updates that have helped to make the shoe—at least according to Nike—lighter and more efficient.

The newly introduced version of the Atomknit upper is a fine mesh that’s more substantial than it looks. Unlike some other top-end super shoes, Nike didn’t skimp on the outsole, with plenty of rubber coverage on the bottom. The carbon fiber plate is wider, too, and the shoe overall is roomier than previous iterations.

Still, the Alphafly 4 weighs in at about 6.6 ounces, which is on the lighter end for a mainline racing shoe (but not the lightest on the market). The foam formulation is also new; the top layer is called ZoomX LT, which Nike claims is lighter and provides more energy return than the standard ZoomX, which is below the plate. That foam is stacked to 39 mm, with an 8 mm drop.

Sources indicate that AS I BEGAN my NYC marathon run, I could feel the Alphafly 4’s combination of plate, foam, and rocker ramping up underfoot for a fast day. The push off the pavement was effortless, and the combination of the perfect weather and unmatched vibes of the crowd made it easy to surge ahead of my target pace. But I wasn’t gunning for a PR (this was my third major race of the year, and I was more focused on maintaining a balanced pace and testing the self-serve water stations than pushing my limits).

I dialed back my excitement as I crossed the Verrazzano Bridge from the start on Staten Island, a spot that’s notorious for gassing overhyped runners leading off the race, and I was able to settle into a comfortable groove. The Alphafly 4 brought a good balance; I felt it was somewhere between the ultra-propulsive super shoes that have lately dominated the elite racing circuit and the more approachable carbon plate shoes that aren’t able to quite keep up.

As I continued along the course, I was pleased with the consistent ride. I wasn’t exerting a ton of energy through my stride, but I was still cruising through the miles. The grippy outsole paid off as I sloshed through the water stations area, crunching crushed cups without altering my gait. I was able to just cycle my legs from step to step, allowing the rebound to push me forward.

According to recent reports, when I ran the Boston Marathon earlier in the year, one of my biggest problems was the pounding my feet took on the back end of the course. I was in pain for days after, and lost my first ever toenail. As I pushed through Mile 20 and above during my NYC run, I kept expecting the pain to come. While my legs did grow heavy and my pace dropped off, my feet didn’t experience the same amount of punishment. The Alphafly 4 isn’t specifically meant for folks with wide feet by any means, but the wider base was much kinder to my tired dogs than other models I’ve worn for 26.2. I finished the race on a high note pushing for the final stretch, propelled along in part thanks to the extra push I could depend on from the shoe.

Sources indicate that THE ALPHAFLY 4 will be a reliable racer for lots of runners who want speed on the roads without going to the extremes. I appreciated the comfortable fit and smooth ride through my own race, and the propulsion provided a nice balance between less aggressive super shoes and the pace-pushing pinnacle “hyper” shoes that have started to emerge, like Puma’s Fast-R Nitro 3, Adidas’ record-breaking Pro Evo 3, and Nike’s own Apex model, which took the top spot at the NYC marathon and replaces the Alphafly line at the top of the brand’s racing stable.

Sources indicate that still, less experienced runners and those who expect to take four or more hours to finish a marathon might find this to be a bit too much shoe. There are other options that will both be less expensive and friendlier to slower paces. The $280 price puts the Alphafly 4 just $5 more than the comparable Adidas Adios Pro 5 (and it’s actually $5 less at launch than the Alphafly 3). Now that there are more levels of quality for super shoes, rather than just one premier shoe per brand, costs closer to $300 seem to be the norm.

It has been revealed that overall, Nike has done a solid job continuing the Alphafly legacy—there are just way more super-powered racers around now than in the early days of super shoes. Still, the model is going to work for lots of runners. If you’re chasing a goal time and you need something that can be both fast and wearable, the Alphafly 4 is going to be one of your absolute top picks.

Brett Williams, NASM-CPT, PES, a senior editor at Men's Health, is a certified trainer and former pro football player and tech reporter. You can find his work elsewhere at Mashable, Thrillist, and other outlets.

Recent findings suggest that sheets get slept in every night and washed every week (in theory) which means it doesn’t take long to learn which ones hold up under use. Every retailer here comes recommended by an AD editor or contributor who has lived with the bedding at home for a long stretch: flannel kept on the bed through May, linen hauled to a communal laundromat and back, or a sheet set that survives a dog digging in every night.

Each brand earned its spot for a reason, whether that’s price, a cooling fabric, an unusually wide color range, or embroidery done by hand. Rest assured: they’re all comfy.

Sources indicate that for bedding basics that won’t damage the budget, Quince is our first stop. Its European Linen Sheet Set earned our pick for the best affordable linen sheets, and senior shopping editor Nashia Baker has recently added the brand to her list of favorites. “The price point is unbeatable, and I love that they offer bedding sets in beautiful colorways and a variety of fabric options,” she says. “The quality is also impressive, especially considering the affordability.”.

Made from 100% European flax, the sheets cost a fraction of what competitors charge, thanks in part to Quince’s direct-to-consumer model which skips traditional retail markups. “I love its airy nature along with the gorgeous Bordeaux color that complements the rest of my decor,” notes Baker. The bedding range extends to quilts and coverlets, , and the brand’s down comforter also made our ranking of the best comforters.

According to recent reports, anyone who has paused a Nancy Meyers movie to study the bedroom should start with Serena & Lily. The brand is based in Sausalito, California, but its textured, breezy bedding and decor would look right at home on any coast, Nantucket included. The range covers lightweight linen and crisp cotton percale in pale colors and easygoing prints.

Sources indicate that of all the bedding Baker has tested, the Nantucket Stripe Sheet Set ranks near the top for its light weight and “worn-in texture,” which keeps the linen soft instead of scratchy. The ruffle trim keeps her bed from looking too plain. “The striped mink print does give a seaside vibe, but it’s been neutral enough to layer with any color bed cover without clashing with the rest of my minimal, romantic decor over the few months I’ve tested the set,” she adds. For a top layer, there’s the scalloped Baywood Quilt, which Alpert likes as a light blanket for “when you want to throw something over while you read your favorite Emily Henry book in bed.”.

Sources indicate that boll & Branch sheets arrive feeling as if they’ve already been through several wash cycles, without the fraying or pilling that usually comes with that. Contributor Rachel Fletcher tested the brand’s percale, Supima cotton, flannel, and linen, but its signature sateen stood out most for its long-staple cotton and a soft, smooth finish. “That extra-soft feel, paired with the lovely, cooling properties, make them feel like the luxury sheets they are,” she says. Converts can outfit the rest of the room too, with Boll & Branch’s mattresses and bedroom furniture.

Brooklinen started out selling two things, cotton percale and sateen sheets, and has since added cashmere, brushed flannel, and a long list of prints. Pieces come in bundled sets or one at a time, and prices land between the budget brands and the luxury labels. Our editors keep coming back to the linen sheets, which they use in every season.

Sources indicate that “Since I don’t live my life on a Greek island, I thought white linen sheets year-round might be a slightly bold move, but the nature of the fiber is versatile and temperature regulating,” indicates AD contributor Madeleine Luckel, who tested the Core Sheet Set. Fletcher sleeps on the Luxe Sheet Set and credits it with keeping her cool. “I’m a hot sleeper with sensitive skin, and they’re really cool on my skin at night, which is a huge relief,” she says. “I love the breathability of these sheets.”.

Few bedding brands have tied their name to sustainability as closely as Coyuchi. Its linen sheets are made from certified organic French flax grown without synthetic fertilizers or pesticides, and the brand also offers percale, sateen, and flannel sheets. The earthy color palette is a selling point on its own.

Sources indicate that “I love the color, which is what drew me to these sheets in the first place,” says Sam Cochran, global features editor. “They’re the perfect brown—a tad auburn, ever so slightly timeworn in palette.”.

In a recent development, shopping writer Julia Harrison and contributor Kate McGregor agree: Garnet Hill is their “secret spot” for bedding. Harrison is devoted to the flannel sheets and admits she leaves them on the bed through May because “they’re so soft, I’d rather suffer in my own sweat than switch them out.” The ticking stripe is “perfectly classic—like a true vintage piece, but not actually vintage…that might be tough sell in the bedding department.” Alpert also loves her flannel pick, a duvet cover that “signals a cottagecore moment without going over the top.” Paired with her Ostermoor duvet insert, it’s “like climbing under a layer of meringue.” Garnet Hill specializes in vintage-inspired designs, patchwork quilts especially, made in 100% linen and 100% cotton options at reasonable prices.

Sources indicate that cozy Earth makes breathable bedding for people who run hot at night, and its signature bamboo bedding, made of 100% viscose, are the brand’s best-known example. “I honestly thought these sheets were silk,” says contributor Megan Wahn. “That’s how smooth and soft they feel.” Wahn tested them mostly in winter, and despite feeling cool to the touch, they kept her warm. “I’m especially eager to see how they perform in the summer,” she adds. “Something about their smoothness makes me think the summer-night sweats won’t stand a chance.”.

Industry observers note that parachute is where we send anyone after classic, well-made cotton bedding. Its sets and bundles are designed with sustainability in mind, and the percale and brushed cotton are made by artisans at the brand’s factory in Portugal.

According to recent reports, “We love [Parachute] because the bedding is designed to provide a hotel-like experience, offering a perfect balance of softness and crispness,” notes Stephanie Kraus of Stephanie Kraus Designs, whose clients favor the brand’s linen bedding sets. “They become softer with each wash while maintaining their durability and are super soft to sleep in every night.”.

According to recent reports, fletcher also praises the brand’s commitment to organic, ethically sourced materials; the Organic Cloud Cotton Duvet Set, for one, is made of Oeko-Tex-certified 100% cotton. “I try a lot of bedding in this line of work and the more I do, the more I appreciate ethical and organic production, even if the price tag is a little higher,” she claims.

Recent findings suggest that greenRow makes charming, long-lasting bedding from recycled and sustainably sourced materials, and it has won over several people on the Shop AD team. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert calls the Helena Floral Sheet Set “without a doubt, the softest sheets I own.” She compares the cotton satin to velvet, and the butter-yellow florals and green micro-gingham ruffle make the set prettier still. McGregor, meanwhile, is partial to the reversible patchwork quilt. “It’s the kind of blanket that feels substantial without trapping heat or feeling stuffy,” she notes. “I feel cocooned without a down comforter, but I’m not smothered when I sleep sans AC in the warmer months. It’s a year-round bedding piece for me, especially since the color palette can lean moodier or more cheerful depending on my sheet selection.”.

Rebecca Udall is a newer name and one worth knowing. Her namesake bedding line is built on romantic, careful details, such as soft-colored decorative embroidery along the sheets. McGregor’s current favorite is this scalloped percale sheet set. “The feel is like a washed percale, crisp but forgiving, and I find that the subtle color on the detailed edge gives the perfect amount of visual interest to my all-white bedscape,” she says. If you want less ornament, try the Georgiana duvet cover, with faint ladderstitch detailing hand-embroidered by artisans in Northern Italy.

In a recent development, hommey, an Australian brand founded in 2020, first caught on with its boldly striped robes and nightwear. It has since carried those designs into cotton and linen sheets and duvet covers. Across both fabrics, there are more than two dozen colors and prints to choose from. For maximalists who want to try color-blocking, the brand’s bolder colorways are a great place to start.

Industry observers note that baker tested the brown sugar linen duvet cover and found the stonewashed, Oeko-Tex certified flax smoother and more broken-in straight out of the package than the Quince version she already owned (above). “I won’t get ahead of myself and say it feels like pure silk, but I can confirm that it’s soft and breathable almost like an organic cotton duvet after a few washes,” Baker says. She pairs the chocolatey shade with burgundy linen sheets for a moodier bed, though it also works as a neutral with lighter sheets in oatmeal, which pick up the cream trim. The one drawback is that the cover has no interior ties, so the insert can shift around inside.

It has been revealed that australian brand Cultiver makes linen sheets and duvets with an easy, beachy look. Its Oeko-Tex certified pieces are an investment, and a worthwhile one. Coverlets are generously sized so they drape loosely, and the envelope-back pillow cases hold their shape without looking stiff. Fletcher has put her set through heavy use and many wash cycles. “Linen is my bedding fabric of choice pretty much 365 days a year, and Cultiver’s high-quality sheet sets do it for me in a way no other brand has. Out of all the sets I’ve tried, this one has stood the test of many washes, my dog digging in them to get cozy at night, and surviving across seasons without feeling worn or threadbare,” she states.

Erica Tanov’s bedding is handmade by artisans in Jaipur, in 100% linen with embroidery drawn from traditional Indian textiles. Harrison calls hers “a lifetime set” that “draws more compliments than anything else in my apartment.” The linen is soft and tough: She hauls this sheet set to her neighborhood laundromat, and it survives the communal machines without damage. It’s the first linen set she’s found to be “city-friendly,” as she calls it. She hasn’t tried the quilts or throw blankets yet, though one already tops her birthday wishlist (this one).

It depends mostly on how you like your bed to feel and how reliable your thermostat is. If you like the crisp coolness of hotel sheets, try percale. If you like a soft, organic feel, try linen for a breezy texture, or bamboo sheets for something similar to silk. Cotton sheets (like Supima sets) are often the most durable over time, especially after many, many washes. Your warmest options are generally flannel sets, and your coolest are generally bamboo and percale. For a basic setup, we recommend a full sheet set (flat sheet included, people) plus a duvet insert with a cover. The cover protects the insert and keeps it clean, so you’ll generally only need to wash the insert every six months rather than weekly like your sheets. Harrison likes to go one step further with a bed blanket underneath her duvet and above her sheets for a bit of weight and additional warmth. If a fluffy duvet isn’t your thing, a quilt or coverlet can take its place and add a little more weight.

What to Look for When Buying Bedding.

Start with the fiber content on the label. Search for 100% cotton, linen (the more organic, the better), and steer clear of polyesters or more plastic fibers, as they’re likely to pill more swiftly and break apart in the washer and dryer.

#110693. How To Build Strength You’ll Actually Use In Daily Life, According To A Trainer

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (650 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

How To Build Strength You’ll Actually Use In Daily Life, According To A Trainer

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that strength training isn't just about what you can lift in the gym.
  • As we get older, we naturally start to lose muscle mass, strength and bone density—at approximately 3-8% per decade after the age of 30—but regular strength training can help slow this down, reminds Andy Carr, trainer and head of fitness for Snap Fitness UK.
  • Thankfully, you don't need complicated exercises to see the benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that strength training isn't just about what you can lift in the gym. It helps make everyday tasks easier, whether that's carrying heavy shopping bags and moving furniture or putting a suitcase in the overhead compartment on a flight.

As we get older, we naturally start to lose muscle mass, strength and bone density—at approximately 3-8% per decade after the age of 30—but regular strength training can help slow this down, reminds Andy Carr, trainer and head of fitness for Snap Fitness UK.

Thankfully, you don't need complicated exercises to see the benefits.

By focusing on simple, functional movements that mimic everyday activities, you can build strength that carries over into daily life and keeps you strong, active and confident as you get older.

Industry observers note that “It's not necessary to spend hours lifting weights to build strength that makes a difference,” he explains. “Even two or three strength sessions a week can help, especially when you're focusing on compound exercises that work several muscle groups at once.”.

Squats are one of the best exercises for building lower-body strength because—as a compound exercise—they work your thighs, glutes, and core all at once.

“These are the muscles you use when getting up from a chair, lifting something off the floor or crouching down to do some gardening,” indicates Carr. Keeping them strong can make a real difference to how easily you move around, particularly as you get older.

Step-ups are great for building leg strength and improving balance at the same time, claims Carr.

Industry observers note that “They're particularly useful for everyday activities like climbing stairs, walking uphill, or stepping onto curbs. As we age, maintaining strength and stability in our legs becomes increasingly key, and step-ups are a simple way to work on both,” he adds.

Farmer's carries are a brilliant exercise for building strength you actually use, because they're essentially the same movement as carrying heavy shopping bags.

“They work your grip, shoulders and core, helping you carry things more comfortably and with better stability. Grip strength can decline with age, so it's a really useful exercise to include in your routine,” notes Carr.

In a recent development, picking something up, whether it's a laundry basket, a suitcase or a bag of compost in the garden, involves your glutes, hamstrings, and back. Deadlifts strengthen all these muscles, explains Carr.

“They're a great way to build strength for everyday lifting, so those jobs feel easier and you're more confident handling heavier objects.”.

Rows are ideal for strengthening your upper back and arms, which we use for pulling movements throughout the day, from opening heavy doors to pulling a garden hose across the lawn.

“They also help support good posture, particularly if you spend a lot of time sitting at a desk,” indicates Carr. “Using a resistance band makes it easy to adjust the difficulty as you get stronger.”.

Incline push-ups are a great way to build upper-body strength, working your chest, shoulders, arms, and core.

“These muscles help with everyday pushing movements, whether that's moving a shopping cart, pushing open a heavy door, or getting yourself up from the floor,” indicates Carr.

They're also easy to adapt to your fitness level, so you can gradually increase the challenge as your strength improves.

We use rotational movements more than we probably realize, whether that's turning to put something in the back of the car, reaching across to pick something up or digging in the garden.

Woodchops are great for strengthening your core and improving your ability to twist and turn with control, Carr explains.

“That becomes particularly useful as we get older, helping us stay mobile and making everyday movements feel easier.”.

In a recent development, kate puts together fitness content that covers functional and strength training, cardio, workout challenges, interviews and news. She's often doing gym laundry or listening to music.

Is Yeti’s Upcoming Performance Outdoor Clothing Any Good? I Put It to the Test to Find Out.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1688 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • IN A SURPRISE move not many saw, Yeti recently launched a performance outdoor clothing line.
  • We put three signature garments from the latest five-piece line to test: The Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket, the Tilloo Hooded Rain Jacket, and the Sansaba Fleece 260 Full-Zip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IN A SURPRISE move not many saw, Yeti recently launched a performance outdoor clothing line. It’s a deviation, sure, but perhaps a sensible one given the brand’s commitment to outdoor gear and all things insulation. As frequent testers of new products in this ever-expanding category, we could not resist the chance to throw them on and put them through the paces in the elements.

We put three signature garments from the latest five-piece line to test: The Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket, the Tilloo Hooded Rain Jacket, and the Sansaba Fleece 260 Full-Zip. For context, the other two pieces are the Caprock Merino Quarter-Zip and the Heuco 310 Full-Zip, essentially siblings of the fleece we tried out. To the brand’s credit, no PFAs are used in the line and all items come with a three-year warranty.

Before even testing, there’s plenty to be intrigued by. The pieces show some clear restraint from a brand that tends toward boldness and large logos (you know, like the beloved coolers). You’d barely even know these were Yeti tops, as you really have to hunt for the brand stamp. And there’s a less-is-more approach in the design here, clearly made with active lifestyles and packability in mind (even color-wise, there are only two options max per item, a somewhat refreshing factoid).

I tried all three pieces over a couple of weeks in the dead of fall in the Pacific Northwest. Translation? They were subjected to downpours, foggy night jogs, chilly mornings, and windy afternoons. I wore them on long walks with the dog, bike commutes in the rain, adventures on muddy trails, and to evening soccer games. I even brought them to the coast during a storm that stirred up high surf and sideways precipitation. Here’s what I think after all the initial testing.

According to recent reports, the Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket looks good, there’s no denying as much. The sleek, trim fit works for even the most active functions and we found it never overheated in testing. Lightweight and packable, it’s somewhat nimble thanks to two-way stretch fabric but not as much so as the other two items tested.

Recent findings suggest that the water resistance is also impressive. I walked the dog through a downpour in this jacket for about 30 minutes and came back with just a few moisture spots on my layer beneath. Not bad for a jacket that certainly doesn’t claim to be waterproof (though does sport a water-repellant finish). In drizzle and light rain, you’re just fine in this puffer jacket. In fact, the water would bead up with the same intensity even after many wears, meaning that exterior was done right.

Recent findings suggest that while I liked the felt-lined pockets, I think they could be even warmer. The blend of Expedry Down and traceable European Lavalan Wool insulation is perhaps the jacket’s strongest feature. Going with a hybrid blend affords an ability to tightrope walk that fine-line between breathability and protection from the elements—and the proof was in the performance.

At $400 though, this is not a cheap item by any stretch of the imagination.

This was my favorite piece of the trio, and arguably the most straightforward. From the superior YKK Aquaguard zipper to the extremely packable nature of the jacket, the Tilloo is a genuine winner. Like a significant boss in your favorite video game, so many jackets in the category have a weak spot hidden somewhere. It usually translates to water seeping in from a cuff or finding its way in through an average zipper. Not here—this jacket is watertight yet breathable.

It has been revealed that one of the coolest features is just how quiet this jacket is. As somebody born and raised in the Pacific Northwest, I’ve worn a fair number of waterproof shells. Many of them swish loudly as you move (not unlike Jim Carrey in Dumb and Dumber as he’s pretending to run while driving). This less crinkly option is quite quiet, a bonus you perhaps never knew you desired (but once you have it, it’s hard to go back).

According to recent reports, if you’re like me, you like to get outdoors to get away from all the noise. A loud jacket can disrupt an adventure, whether you’re birding in a marsh or scanning for wildlife on a hike. This jacket is not silent but it’s noticeably more hushed than most others, even during animated motions and heavy exercise. The Velcro cuffs create nice clasps over base layers (or just above a smartwatch during a run) while the liner itself is fairly soft to the touch, unlike the less appealing, membrane-like feel you get from so many options. The hood is adjustable and offers a nice panorama without hampering much of your view. And the way it pulls rain off is impressive, meaning you never have to shake off pooling areas like you might with a lesser jacket or umbrella.

Industry observers note that it has become my go-to for offseason excursions. While $350 is an undeniable expense, the jacket is worth the price.

Straight on, the Sansaba Fleece 260 is incredibly soft (like, you’re gonna want to nuzzle it). The proprietary PrimaLoft Bio Fleece is a sensory joy, with a lovely feel and a density level that seems to hit the Goldilocks spot. Best, it’s a composite of 100% post-consumer recycled materials. These shorter fibers are densely distributed, creating what Yeti classifies as a midweight garment. We’d argue that it performs on the higher end of the spectrum, at least in terms of insulation and warmth. No, it wouldn’t quite cut it on its own for significant stretches in below-freezing conditions, but it does just find in the kind of cold we’re normally subjected to.

The fleece also breathes quite well. I found that it paired nicely with a brisk mountain hike or even a sweaty workout in damp conditions. However, playing under anything more than a light drizzle requires a proper shell to fend off precipitation. We liked the length of the collar, stylish yet still major enough to hide under during chilly gusts of wind.

Billed as a fleece made for movement and strenuous activities, the Sansaba fared pretty well. I really put it to the sword one day, zipping it up for a four-mile run in light rain. Normally, I’d wear a long-sleeve moisture-wicking shirt beneath, but I wanted to see how the fleece would fare atop a regular cotton T-shirt. While it did well at fending off light moisture and pulling some of the sweat from my arms, I was pretty soaked in sweat at the end. A pretty easy fix with a better undershirt, sure, but it indicates that perhaps the fleece can’t quite do the most strenuous activities without an unwanted side effect (props for drying so quickly after the fact, however).

Additional cons? The interior of the pockets could use some work. The plain mesh is boring and doesn’t do much to warm the paws. But the fleece is so warm and welcoming throughout the top that you can just rest your hands elsewhere for a quick warm-up. The collar also hugs the neck nicely. This is bittersweet, as it really cradles the area and keeps it warm; however, if you like to duck your chin and mouth (and a little nose) beneath this part of a top during a wind gust, it’s harder to do as it’s fairly snug. For $180, this is a pretty good deal, but not necessarily superior to several other fleeces at a similar price point.

While you don’t need the whole set, you might want a few of these pieces to bolster your outdoor apparel game. I recommend them all, but with some caveats. The rain jacket is the best item for the price and is very much on par with others in the category.

The puffer is nice but I don’t find it a whole lot better than, say, this one from Wren that I’ve been wearing for a couple of years now (the Columbia Terwilliger Treail Heat Seal Jacket is another fine option). The neat, textured, and non-glossy (per so, so many) look is hard to beat, but it’s a significant chunk of change even give its merits.

Recent findings suggest that the fleece is also an attractive piece of outerwear with some high-performance capabilities, but perhaps not at the same level as some of its counterparts at its decidedly high price point. I tends toward options like the Patagonia Better Jacket and the Trailmade from REI, a bargain-and-a-half. But the Sansaba is an undoubtedly good-looking option with a lot going for it.

Yeti is clearly on to something here and has turned heads with a combination of clean fits, useful tech, and designs with mobility in mind (not to mention some environmentally conscious moves too). But this writer would suggest splurging on perhaps just one of the items depending on your adventuring angles and lifestyle.

Yeti Sansaba Fleece 260 Full-Zip.

Yeti Caprock Merino 250 Quarter-Zip.

#110691. Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1438 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging.
  • It has been revealed that when Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month. But there’s a problem buyers should know about: they won’t be able to charge it at home.

Recent findings suggest that the Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging. And the wireless home charging pad Tesla has been teasing since 2023 still isn’t something you can buy.

It has been revealed that when Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug. “It just goes over the inductive charger and charges,” he said on stage.

It has been revealed that that plan didn’t survive production, or at least the current version in production. Cybercabs have a NACS charge port behind a panel in the rear bumper, and Tesla has been plugging Cybercabs into regular Superchargers in Austin since they joined the fleet.

The bigger matter is what sits behind that port. Tesla confirmed to attendees at Tesla’s Austin launch event in September that Cybercab has no onboard charger, the box that turns the AC power coming out of your wall into DC power the battery can store.

No onboard charger means no Wall Connector. No Mobile Connector on a 120V outlet, and no Level 2 station at the mall either. If it isn’t a DC fast charger, the Cybercab can’t use it.

According to recent reports, for a robotaxi, deleting the onboard charger makes sense. It’s one less part to buy, cool, and carry around, and a fleet car spends its downtime at a depot, not in someone’s garage. Those little things help make the car more economical and efficient.

But Tesla is now selling the Cybercab to individuals.

In a recent development, as we reported last week, Tesla’s Cybercab autonomy agreement requires a $299 monthly subscription for the car to move at all. The same document puts charging squarely on the buyer: “You are responsible for registration, insurance, parking, charging, general cleaning and all other costs.”.

It also tells owners to “keep the vehicle charged and connected so over-the-air updates can install.” Connected to what, it doesn’t say.

The Cybercab Order Agreement limits the car to NACS DC fast charging, Superchargers included. It also claims only the registered owner can use the Cybercab, and only while physically present in it for the entire trip.

The subscription agreement carves out one exception: when service is due, the Cybercab “will travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center.” Nothing similar exists for charging.

Sources indicate that so you can’t send your Cybercab to a Supercharger at 2 a.m. while you sleep, which is the one thing a self-driving car should be great at. You’d have to ride along, sit in a two-seater at a Supercharger while it charges, and ride back home.

The obvious answer is the wireless home charger Tesla keeps promising.

Industry observers note that tesla first showed what looked like a wireless home charging station during its Investor Day in March 2023. Later that year, chief designer Franz von Holzhausen confirmed the project on Jay Leno’s Garage, saying owners would “just drive over the pad in your garage” to start charging.

Tesla then filed patents for the charging pad and, after the Cybercab unveiling, released a video of it charging the robotaxi at 25 kW, claiming efficiency “well above 90%.” In February, the FCC granted Tesla a waiver to use ultra-wideband radios to guide the Cybercab onto the pad.

In a recent development, and that’s where it stops. Tesla has never sold the pad, never priced it, and never given it a launch date. It even gave up on wireless charging for the Cybertruck last year, even though the truck shipped with the connectors for it.

With deliveries estimated for December, Tesla has about six weeks to launch a home pad if it wants the first owners to charge in their own garage.

According to recent reports, tesla’s own plans for Cybercab charging revolve around fleet depots. In Austin, it filed plans for a hub on St. Elmo Road with 48 V4 Supercharger stalls in a first phase and cabinets to support 80 wireless chargers in a second.

Tesla could, in theory, let private owners use it. But with the owner-presence rule, that means riding to a depot across town and waiting there. That’s a Supercharger visit with extra steps.

Industry observers note that the other route is a home DC charger, and those exist. We covered Sigenergy’s 25 kW bidirectional DC charging module last year, which bypasses a car’s onboard charger the same way a Supercharger does. Lunar Energy also unveiled a 25 kW home DC charger this year, but it’s not expected until mid-2027.

Recent findings suggest that neither is a plug-and-play answer. Sigenergy’s module is built to sit inside its SigenStor home battery system, which isn’t cheap, and Tesla would have to support third-party DC charging on a car it controls this tightly. Tesla could also build its own small DC wall unit. It hasn’t revealed one, but CEO Elon Musk talked about integrating one into the Powerwall for years.

Industry observers note that this is what happens when you take a vehicle designed for a fleet and sell it to consumers to hit a deadline. And let’s be honest, charging is probably not even in the top 5 of problems with selling the Cybercab to personal owners in its current state.

Sources indicate that musk promised a Cybercab would be sold to a customer for under $30,000 before 2027. Technically, he’s going to make it. But on the Q3 earnings call, he also stated “the vast majority” of Cybercabs will stay Tesla-owned and run as transport-as-a-service. The car was clearly engineered around that, and deleting the onboard charger is the best example.

Recent findings suggest that that saved Tesla money on every unit. The cost now lands on the few people buying one.

I don't see any evidence that the production Cybercab has the onboard hardware to use such a pad. Besides the wireless receiver coil it would need some kind of charging hardware to convert the pulsed wireless charging into DC to charge the battery.

If you live in Austin next to a Supercharger, you’ll manage. But think about what Tesla is actually selling here: a self-driving car that can’t drive itself to charge, can’t charge in your garage, and needs you sitting in it at a Supercharger. That’s worse than owning a Model 3 with a Wall Connector, and it costs $299 a month on top.

In a recent development, the fix exists in Tesla’s labs. It has the pad, the patents, and the FCC approval. It needs to ship it as a product, ideally bundled with the car, or change the contract to let the Cybercab go charge on its own.

In a recent development, will the first Cybercab owners get a wireless pad in December, or will they spend their evenings at Superchargers? And if it rolls out, how much will it cost? The rare few home wireless chargers that have been sold to date have been quite expensive, and the value proposition of the Cybercab, which is presently basically a $300 a month lease with a $30,000 down payment, is already pretty awful.

#110689. Can squirrels really survive any fall?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1115 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Can squirrels really survive any fall?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On any ordinary day, you might witness the breathtaking display of squirrels high in the trees, doing what seems like effortless, daredevilish parkour.
  • A large, heavy human being attempting these same maneuvers would likely fall—and would be looking at a trip to the E.R., at best.
  • Yet squirrels, it seems, tend to walk away from these situations unscathed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On any ordinary day, you might witness the breathtaking display of squirrels high in the trees, doing what seems like effortless, daredevilish parkour. They might launch themselves off one branch, bounce off another, and somehow reorient themselves in midair like it’s nothing.

A large, heavy human being attempting these same maneuvers would likely fall—and would be looking at a trip to the E.R., at best.

Yet squirrels, it seems, tend to walk away from these situations unscathed. You’ve probably even heard that squirrels can survive a fall from any height. But according to Dr. Nathaniel Hunt of the University of Nebraska at Omaha, this comes with an important caveat: Even these brazen little gymnasts don’t stick the landing every single time.

In a recent development, “I would put an asterisk on the claim that squirrels can survive a fall from literally any height,” Hunt tells Popular Science. “Their size makes large falls surprisingly survivable, but they are not invulnerable.”.

So, can squirrels survive, if not all, most falls? And if so, how?

It’s much more than luck that keeps squirrels landing safely; they are no more immune than we are to the laws of gravity. It’s what happens in the air—both in terms of their anatomical engineering and their instincts—that allows them to survive most falls and get right back to their nut-hiding hijinks.

It has been revealed that according to Hunt, a falling squirrel faces three challenges: the speed of the fall, its orientation midair, and the impact when it lands. A squirrel’s small body helps; at about a pound, a squirrel weighs about as much as a loaf of bread.

It has been revealed that “Being small gives it a lot of aerodynamic area relative to its weight, so air resistance limits its speed,” Hunt claims. “It also has much less kinetic energy than a larger animal.”.

It has been revealed that so, squirrels’ light and small bodies help them hit the ground with less force, but that’s not all that’s going on. Hunt says squirrels instinctively know how to move through the air and land on the ground, which helps to optimize their already “favorable physics.” The tail is a key player in these midair maneuvers.

Sources indicate that “The tail is more interesting than a fluffy parachute,” Hunt notes. “At low airspeeds, aerodynamic forces are small, but the squirrel can still use inertial tail movements to exchange angular momentum with the body and control orientation.” In other words, squirrels use their tail to control how and where they fall.

Recent findings suggest that research backs Hunt’s claim. A 2021 study found that squirrels experiencing unexpected falls were able to rapidly rotate their tails, a motion that caused the rest of their bodies to rotate in the opposite direction. Hunt compared the role of the tail to that of a “reaction wheel” on a spacecraft.

“Accelerating the tail in one direction helps rotate or stabilize the body in the other direction,” Hunt says.

As a squirrel’s fall picks up speed, the tail may function more like the feathers on an arrow, Hunt suggests. If the squirrel starts to veer off course, the airflow pushes against the tail just enough to redirect its body into a stable position. Even then, the tail isn’t acting like a true parachute; instead of slowing the squirrel’s descent, the tail is nudging its body in the right direction.

Size, anatomy, and aerial reorientation are all important to a squirrel’s seemingly magical ability to survive most falls. However, there’s a third skill that plays an equally important part, one Hunt thinks may be “the most underappreciated part of the story.” Squirrels know how to come in for a landing.

“A recent study I co-authored found that fox squirrels managed more than 80 percent of their landing energy through their forelimbs,” Hunt claims of a study looking at squirrels leaping between branches. “They also adjusted their forces depending on whether they undershot or overshot the branch.”.

According to recent reports, in other words, a landing isn’t just something that happens to a squirrel. On some level, they’re doing damage control.

“They are not simply hitting the branch,” Hunt says. “They are actively controlling the collision.”.

So, how slowly does a squirrel have to fall to be able to walk away?

In a recent development, the answer lies in our furry friend’s terminal velocity, the top speed something reaches while falling once air resistance balances gravity’s pull and stops it from accelerating further. Hunt states a squirrel’s terminal velocity can be reasonably estimated at about 20 to 40 mph, depending on its posture, limb position, and tail. For reference, Hunt estimates the terminal velocity of a cat—famous nine lives aside—at about 60 mph, while a belly-down human skydiver is likely to fall at about 120 mph.

“All of these are approximate, because posture matters enormously,” he says.

Posture explains some of the variation, but size is ultimately the main driver. A giant squirrel, therefore, would likely fare much worse in a fall, even with perfect tail control and posture.

“You could not simply build a squirrel 10 times larger and expect it to tolerate the same fall,” Hunt notes.

It has been revealed that likewise, a squirrel’s comparatively slow terminal velocity doesn’t mean it’s out of the proverbial woods. It might seem that once a squirrel hits its maximum speed, height wouldn’t matter much, making a fall from 10 feet and a fall from 100 feet equally survivable. Hunt cautions against assumptions like this.

“Reaching terminal velocity does not make a squirrel immune to injury,” he says. “The landing surface, body orientation, and any collisions along the way still matter.”.

This complex interplay of physics, instinct, learning, and split-second decision-making is part of what makes squirrels a fascinating study subject for Hunt.

“What fascinates me is that you cannot neatly separate ‘the brain’ from ‘the mechanics,'” Hunt claims. “Squirrel agility emerges from sensing, learning, body shape, and physical dynamics working together.”.

#110687. Industry News: Ginger Rogers at Home: 10 Photos of the Golden Age Icon’s Glamorous SoCal Life

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1450 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Architecturaldigest ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Ginger Rogers at Home: 10 Photos of the Golden Age Icon’s Glamorous SoCal Life

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1450 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that while most people race to the hospital to give birth, Ginger Rogers’s mother, Lela, insisted that her baby girl’s first breaths be taken in their Missouri home.
  • Recent findings suggest that decades after her death in 1995, Rogers is poised to return to the significant screen by way of Sabrina Carpenter, who’s set to portray the late actor in the forthcoming, yet-to-be-titled Fred Astaire biopic.
  • Sources indicate that after Rogers separated from her second husband, actor Lew Ayres, in 1936, she and her mother moved in together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while most people race to the hospital to give birth, Ginger Rogers’s mother, Lela, insisted that her baby girl’s first breaths be taken in their Missouri home. “The little four-room house at 100 Moore Street was the perfect choice” for the future icon’s July 1911 welcome to the world, Rogers concluded in her 1991 memoir, Ginger: My Story. The star would go on to live with her extended family in Kansas City at 3306 Bellefountain Street; with her stepfather in Fort Worth at 1510 Cooper Street; and once she became a Hollywood sensation, a sprawling Beverly Hills estate. That joy and sense of peace she found in her childhood residence became a defining feature of her California pad. “It was a fun house, a happy house,” Rogers told Architectural Digest in 1994. “I was never angry when I didn’t have to work, because I liked to stay home so much.”.

Recent findings suggest that decades after her death in 1995, Rogers is poised to return to the significant screen by way of Sabrina Carpenter, who’s set to portray the late actor in the forthcoming, yet-to-be-titled Fred Astaire biopic. Tom Holland will star as Astaire. Read on for a glimpse inside the Oscar winner’s off-set life in the places she cherished most.

Rogers on the diving board in 1938.

Sources indicate that after Rogers separated from her second husband, actor Lew Ayres, in 1936, she and her mother moved in together. “I asked Mother if she would like me to build her a house, and if she did, could I live in it with her,” Rogers wrote in her memoir. “The next day she scoured the area for a suitable place to build. She found a wonderful lot high in Beverly Hills on 2.75 acres on Gilcrest Drive in Coldwater Canyon. It had a view that didn’t stop; when the fog burned off late every afternoon, it was possible to see Catalina.” Rogers is pictured at the stunning estate in this 1938 photo.

The actor with her home ice cream fountain.

The Swing Time star added many personal touches to the home, one of which was an elaborate soda fountain. In this 1940 photo, she’s shown whipping up a sweet treat. In her memoir, Rogers recalled all the amenities she installed. “The building took over a year because of labor strikes and material shortages,” she wrote. “When the house was finished, it proved to have been worth waiting for. It had everything I wanted or needed in a house: swimming pool, tennis court, projection room, and my very own soda fountain. Who could ask for anything more?”.

Rogers opened her home tennis court to championship hopefuls so they could get practice matches in.

Rogers was an avid tennis player. Though she’s pictured here in 1950 at her Malibu beach house, the actor also had a home court installed at Gilcrest Drive. “On the way to the pool and tennis court were eight sculptured bay leaf trees. Next to the blue-tiled pool was my tennis court. This was my pride and joy,” she wrote in Ginger: My Story. With the knowledge that Rogers had the only en-tout-cas court in the area, the Tennis Association “begged” her to invite young hopefuls for some practice before they went on to championship matches at Forest Hills, Latest York. “I was delighted to open my court to competitors like Pancho Gonzales, Gussie Moran; and, later, Billie Jean King, Jennifer Hood, and Alice Marble slammed a few over the net too,” Rogers said.

Rogers was known for hosting her Hollywood star friends at home in Beverly Hills.

Industry observers note that the Top Hat actor’s Beverly Hills abode was also a hot party spot for Rogers’s A-list friends. “My home was made for entertaining and I gave party after party,” she wrote in her memoir. “Most of them were informal. I’d serve spaghetti and we’d play some night tennis. Alcohol was never served, just cold drinks. One, a mixture of finely crushed ice, 7-Up, and concentrated orange juice, was a real favorite with the tennis crowd.”.

The star had a close relationship with her mother, Lela.

Sources indicate that rogers loved living with her mother, with whom she’s pictured in the circa 1940s portrait on the piano in this 1954 image. The triple threat pushed back against the term “stage mother” in Architectural Digest; she considered her mom to be “my guide and my professor… she was my encyclopedia. She knew what route to take: She helped Lucille Ball along hers too, you know. It would have been hard to have a career without her.” About their Beverly Hills pad, she added, “we both liked the look of a French farmhouse. And I wanted certain specific things: a helpful bath, a tennis court, and my own projection room, where we had eight or ten director’s chairs, so that friends could come over to watch movies.”.

Rogers with a furry friend at home in the 1950s.

The home featured a main house with bedrooms for Rogers and her mom, as well as a guesthouse for visitors. “The house was very bright,” she told Architectural Digest. “I don’t like dark things; even in my clothing, I prefer to be light and colorful—Springtime for Henry has always been my motto,” she explained, referencing the 1934 comedy. In her memoir, Rogers added, “The style was an American farmhouse with Dutch doors opening to cool breezes. The large bay window in the corner of the living room had a view of Beverly Hills and a bit of Los Angeles. Off the living room was a patio for barbecuing on a flagstone area under a beautiful Australian pepper tree. It was a wonderful place to entertain on crisp California nights.”.

Rogers’s home also included a solarium, and bedrooms with scenic views. “On a lower level was an outside entrance to the playroom,” the actor noted in her memoir. “This room had significant windows and comfortable cushions as did the solarium in the hallway to the patio. I read many a book, with apple in hand, buried in those downy cushions.” About her bedrooms, she added, “There were two bedrooms leading from the solarium, one for Lelee [her mother] with a four-posted bed and one for me. My room looked out on the view of Beverly Hills, and I had a beautiful hand-carved mantel for my fireplace.”.

Rogers at work on an oil painting.

In addition to the stage talents for which she became a star, Rogers was also a painter. Her guesthouse also doubled as a studio. “My studio, which could double as a guesthouse, held all the paraphernalia of my hobbies: painting materials, canvases, paintbrushes, turpentine, pencils, and so on,” she wrote in her memoir. “Whenever there was a lull on set, I’d take out my pencil and sketch,” Rogers added. “I had been drawing for a long time and it seemed to come naturally to me. I found it challenging and relaxing. I never studied drawing or painting, I just did it.”.

In her memoir, Rogers recalled a time when she brought her paintings out for a gallery show. “When I’m not working or traveling, my main source of relaxation comes from my painting,” she wrote. “Gallery owners have wanted to have a one-person show of my work, but I never had the time to organize my paintings. Well, now was the time. Gregg Juarez, a gallery owner and friend of mine, arranged for a show and sale at his gallery in Palm Desert. As we were hanging the paintings for display, I realized these were my children—I couldn’t sell them! Gregg told me I had to sell a few so the customers wouldn’t get mad. I managed to put a few up for sale, but couldn’t part with the rest. So now they are joyously hung in my home for all to see.”.

Rogers was 83 years old when she died in 1995 at home in California.

Rogers remained at her home on Gilcrest Drive until 1970, when her mom urged her to sell while she was away working in Europe. “I had been renting it out more than living in it lately, and Mother thought it was financially sound to put it on the market,” the actor wrote in her memoir. “Besides, she noted it needed a latest roof! She handled all the details of the sale…. This was one time I’m not sure Mother knew best. I adored that house on Gilcrest Drive and have regretted selling it ever since.” Rogers died decades later, on April 25, 1995, at her home in Rancho Mirage, per the Los Angeles Times.

#110686. Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (985 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities.
  • Designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat.
  • “Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang remarked in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities. They’ve already experimented with stretching lab-grown human skin over robot faces and with a synthetic hydrogel skin that lets robots really “feel” burns and cuts. Now, a team of engineers at the University of Pennsylvania wants to dig under the skin. In a  study published this week in Advanced Functional Materials, the team describes a highly controllable artificial robot muscle inspired by the small muscles in human eyes and fingers. They put them to the test by having a robot hand strike piano keys at varying intensities and made a set of human eye muscles able to maintain a gaze. It all feels quite uncomfortably adjacent to the 1973 sci-fi film and HBO series Westworld.

Designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat. For starters, most large robots today, especially humanoid ones, rely on bulky, rigid motors and components. That’s fine for more straightforward actions like walking and lifting, but recreating the muscles that move our eyes or fingers requires far more delicate precision. In this case, the engineers needed a material that prioritized flexibility and fine control while staying strong enough to hold up after repeated use. As with many aspects of robotics, tasks that seem quite easy for humans to do are actually often the most difficult tasks for machines. While bipedal robots have been pulling off dance routines and performing acrobatics worth of a Marvel superhero for years, they still fall flat when it comes to something as simple as folding laundry or holding a gaze.

“Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang remarked in a statement.

For their muscle fiber, the team settled on liquid crystal elastomers (LCE) combined with graphene and an embedded ultrathin copper coil. The LCE, a rubber-like material, acts as the actual muscle, both contracting and stretching. The graphene serves as a reinforcer, making the material both a bit softer and tougher, so it holds up even when opposing muscles pull in other directions. Together, these two ingredients can produce movement, but on their own they struggle to stay put. When heated, the LCE stretches but then keeps contracting, eventually creeping back toward its original length as it rapidly cools. That’s a problem for subtle movements like holding a gaze or pressing a piano key with light, steady force, where the muscle needs to hold a precise position over a period of time.

According to recent reports, that’s where the coil comes in. The team added the coil inside the fiber to serve as a kind of temperature gauge, and the sensors determine when the muscle is losing heat and contracting. With those readings, the team could then gradually increase temperature to ensure the muscle held its position.

“We used the resistance of the embedded copper coil as a feedback signal and adjusted the heating power in real time to keep the resistance near a target value,” added study co-author and University of Pennsylvania Ph.D. student Xuelin Wu. “Because the coil served as both a heater and a sensor, we did not need a separate sensor for feedback.”.

Sources indicate that with their artificial muscle designed, it was time to test it in real-world scenarios. First, the team fitted the muscles into a 3D-printed robot hand built to mimic finger movement. They then made the fingers press various piano keys at different levels of force and speed. Sensors placed on the bottom of the keys were able to tell how hard each note was played. The detached hand was no Mozart, but it worked.

In a recent development, next, they mounted a pair of robotic eyeballs on freely rotating ball joints inside 3D-printed shells. The muscle fibers were attached around the edges of opposing pairs, which were meant to mimic how muscles in the eyes stretch and contract. In testing, the eyes shifted their gaze on demand, with controlled, repeatable movements. The resulting video demonstration is both impressive and unsettling.

In a recent development, the research joins a growing field of labs and companies racing to build artificial muscle systems. In 2025, Polish startup Clone Robotics took the idea to an extreme with a horrifying video of a faceless, human-sized robot dangling from a ceiling and writhing, its movements supposedly powered by synthetic muscles and a hydraulic system meant to mimic human muscles and blood vessels. They call  their creation the world’s first “musculoskeletal android.” Though it is likely that their video was more a shocking proof-of-concept than an actively working prototype, it nonetheless provides a glimpse into a potentially unsettling future where robots replace mechanical motors and actuators with more human-like muscle fibers.

Protoclone, the world's first bipedal, musculoskeletal android. pic.twitter.com/oIV1yaMSyE.

The University of Pennsylvania researchers say the next step is combining more of these muscles into larger, integrated systems, where dozens of small muscles have to work together to produce more natural expressions. Down the line, they’re interested in potentially using AI computer vision to coordinate those into even more complex systems. Authenticity is the point. The long-term goal, they note, is to create robots that look and feel more and more like the real thing.

“I’m excited about the possibility of using this approach to create robots that move with the same subtlety and expressiveness we see in human faces,” concluded University of Pennsylvania engineer and paper co-author Ziyun Zhang.

Volkswagen will reveal the new GTI hot hatch on Friday, promising it will be “something really spicy.”.

To celebrate the GTI’s 50th anniversary, Volkswagen is “starting a upcoming chapter,” with its first all-electric model to bear the iconic performance badge.

Industry observers note that the ID. Polo GTI “brings the legendary GTI driving pleasure into the electric future,” VW stated after opening pre-orders last month.

Volkswagen previewed a mysterious fresh hot hatch draped under a cloth that appears to be a souped-up version of the ID. Polo GTI. Despite its attempt to “hide” it, you can see the massive rear wing and wide wheel arches under the cloth.

The manufacturer promised that “something really spicy” will be served this Friday, November 20, with the tags #Volkswagen, #GTI, and #GTI50.

Although no other details were revealed, the upcoming hot hatch is thought to be the more powerful “Clubsport” variant.

A post shared by Volkswagen (@volkswagen).

Sources indicate that volkswagen’s head of driving dynamics, Florian Umbach, told Autocar earlier this year that the firm is planning to launch the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport, a more powerful variant that will deliver close to 300 hp, up from 223 hp in the standard model.

Umbach noted that Volkswagen is developing “a similar kind of paddleshift power delivery that the Hyundai N cars have” for the upcoming electric hot hatch.

Hyundai’s performance EVs, the IONIQ 5 N and IONIQ 6 N, feature a simulated gear-shifting system called N e-Shift that uses paddle shifters on the steering wheel to replicate the feel of an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission. It works with the N Active Sound+ system to make it feel like you’re in a traditional gas-powered sports car.

Industry observers note that it has yet to be confirmed whether the hot hatch debuting on Friday is, in fact, the latest ID. Polo Clubsport, but the design clues give us a good idea of what’s coming.

Sources indicate that man, $45k for a starting price is a little uncomfortably steep for a hatch, given there are a little bigger options in that range. I wish it started somewhere in the 30s to be competitive.

Check back on Friday for the full details.

Volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, starting at 39,995 euros (about $45,000).

Like the first Golf GTI from 1976, the electric ID. Polo GTI uses a front-wheel-drive powertrain. The front-mounted electric motor delivers 223 hp (166 kW) and 213 lb-ft (290 Nm) of instant torque, enabling it to sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.8 seconds.

In early 2027, Volkswagen will open orders for the ID.3 GTI, the second EV to wear the badge, and its first rear-wheel-drive (RWD) GTI.

WINTER IS QUICKLY approaching. But whether you’re a front-country weekend warrior or a hardcore backcountry camper, you still should have a few camping trips lined up for the year (leaf-peeping fall road trip, anyone?). And it’s never too late to take stock of your gear closet to see what’s missing, what’s busted, and what needs an upgrade.

Recent findings suggest that we cover all the latest and greatest outdoor gear every year in the Men’s Health Outdoor Awards. But, in this guide, we’re covering just the greatest. To offer a wide breadth of options (since there are all different sorts of camping), we’ve broken this guide into categories of tents, sleep systems, kitchen, and general camping gear. Whether it’s all new for 2026 or it’s been around for years, these are our favorite camping and outdoor gear picks for backpacking, car camping, and everything in between—the gear that we love and pack for every trip.

This entry-level tent strikes a good balance of pack weight, affordability, and reliability. It’s roomy enough to sleep two with a dash of gear and sets up faster than most at this price point (even with the included rainfly) for easy-breezy camping in almost any season. Bonus: A limited lifetime warranty.

A generously sized interior, plus oversized doors and vestibules, provides a much more livable space. We love that the hubbed pole design makes for a dead-simple setup and teardown. Plus, Nemo’s commitment to more eco-friendly gear means a bluesign-approved recycled tent floor and PFAS-free rainfly.

So it’s not only a reliable backcountry sleep space, but a day/night lounge when you need it.

Recent findings suggest that the Lunar Solo is a budgversatility for extra gear or your dog. Plus, it’s durable and breathable with solid ventilation. It’s not the single best in any one category, but the price makes it a great all-arounder for weight-conscious backpackers and thru-hikers on a budget. Our main gripes are the tricky setup process and the fact that it requires seam sealing before use—neither of which is a deal breaker at this price point though.

It has been revealed that marmot sought to reinvent the wheel, er, sleeping bag with its all-new Wraptor. The clever design swaps traditional zippers for overlapping flips and magnetic snaps, ensuring a more versatile camp sleep setup. Shed the layers in warmer weather or bundle up when the temperature drops—it’s flexible in every temperature. This same adjustability caters to sleepers who appreciate a “swaddled like a baby” mummy bag and hybrid campers looking for more room to spread out on their stomachs and sides. Also available in a 15-degree option.

According to recent reports, exped’s midrange Terra line is our go-to bag for anyone looking for real, 650-fill-power duck down that’s affordable. The 15-degree temp rating makes this a solid three-season option that’s capable of most four-season camping in all but the coldest weather. It’s comfy enough for car camping, and with a roughly 3-pound pack weight, compact enough for backpacking overnighters. The glow-in-the-dark zipper pull and internal pocket are nifty features, too.

With the Cot One, Helinox creates an instant sleep surface that’s flat, level, comfortable, and off the ground. Fully set up, it’s the perfect front-country camp bed that supports more than 300 pounds. It packs down surprisingly small into the included zip case and weighs less than five pounds. Optional leg extensions are available to lift the cot up to 15 inches off the ground for maximum comfort.

This entry-level model from Wise Owl Outfitters is a great starter option for anyone looking to get into hammock camping or as a budget-friendly “just in case” hammock. The lightweight design weighs less than two pounds for the hammock, straps, carabiners, and stuff sack. It’s surprisingly durable and supports up to 500 pounds. Bonus: It’s available in more than a dozen colors, too.

You typically get what you pay for in the world of inflatable air pads, but Klymit’s Static V Base is something of a unicorn. It’s plenty comfy for front-country camp setups, but it really shines in the backcountry with a compact, featherweight construction that’s surprisingly durable to survive rock punctures and uneven ground. Most impressive? It’s typically available for less than $50.

Sources indicate that we’ll take a proper foam pillow over an inflatable any day. Therm-a-Rest’s fan-favorite compressible relies on an upcycled foam fill and a plush polyester cover for serious front- and backcountry sleep comfort that’s the closest thing to your home bedroom setup. The cinch adjuster (hence the name) allows campers to tweak the pillow’s firmness to their liking. Plus, it packs down to about half its size for easy travel.

For front-country campers with access to electricity (or even a portable power station), Nestout’s Outdoor Cooker adds serious versatility to your outdoor kitchen. The modest 500-watt capability is plenty powerful for cooking rice, boiling, steaming, or whipping up everything from soup to oatmeal. At less than two pounds, it’s compact and lightweight enough to stash in the back of your rig until you need it.

Yeti’s newest cast-iron skillet is also the largest in its lineup. The 14-inch size makes it ideal as an all-in-one pan for car campers looking to pack less cookware. The oversized design comes polished and pre-seasoned, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. An additional grab handle and dual pour spouts make it safer and ultra-versatile for cooking up just about anything.

Industry observers note that this portable fridge from BougeRV is the perfect accompaniment to your existing cooler. Stash the temperature critical foods (meat, eggs, bacon, etc.) in the former and everything else in the latter. It’s small enough to fit in the footwell of most passenger vehicles, and the included 240Wh detachable battery keeps it cold for more than a full day. What’s more: It’s more affordable than most premium midsize coolers.

In a recent development, gerber elevates the lowly spork with the ComplEAT Multi-Fork. It’s the same multipurpose utensil we all know and love, including a deep-basin spoon, a tined fork end, and dual cut/scrape edges. But this premium take adds a six-function multi-tool that clips to the back. So, you also get a serrated package opener, a can opener, a bottle opener, twin flathead drivers, and a pry bar. A clever kickstand feature also keeps the business end up off of dirty rocks and ground.

For campers who value weight and packability above all else, BioLite’s CampStove 2+ is a game-changer. The clever design runs on pretty much any organic material (twigs, pine cones, leaves, wood) to keep it stoked off-grid almost indefinitely. The dual-purpose output charges your phone, GPS, headlamp, and other small devices (at up to three watts) in the backcountry, and it doubles as a stove at mealtime.

Industry observers note that I’m willing to dump a lot of things from my pack to save weight, but coffee isn’t one of them. Sea to Summit’s Frontier Ultralight Collapsible Pour Over is as dead-simple and packable as a camp coffeemaker can get, so you’re guaranteed your morning Joe anywhere. It weighs just two ounces and folds down almost completely flat so you’ll practically forget it’s in your backpack. But it pops open to reveal a legit pour-over coffeemaker that works with most camp and travel mugs.

For serious front-country campers, Jetboil’s Genesis Basecamp is near perfect. The dual-burner system allows for more elaborate meal preparation than single-burner alternatives with up to 10,000 BTU output and maximum flame control. A 5-liter pot and 10-inch ceramic-coated nonstick fry pan are included, so you can prep just about anything for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, even for larger groups.

Recent findings suggest that the all-upcoming Daytrip 20L combines Yeti’s legendary all-day, keep-cold insulation with the portability of a traditional backpack cooler. It’s roomy enough for a six-pack, two lunches, snacks, and an ice pack, making it perfect for day-hike lunch breaks or even as add-on cold storage for weekend trips. A large top opening provides easy access, while external pockets add extra storage for keeping smaller essentials within easy reach.

Recent findings suggest that for long weekends at the campsite or off-grid, we love this oversized cooler from RTIC. The 78-can capacity offers plenty of cold storage for a family getaway, and RTIC’s premium insulation ensures it stays chilled for up to five days. The lightweight design is easier to carry, and all-terrain, puncture-proof wheels make it easy to wheel from the car to the campsite, too.

Car camping is dirty business—literally. That’s why we love simple, versatile adventure storage that just works. Upgrade your existing loadout with this gear box from Gregory. It’s waterproof/dustproof, and the translucent lid makes organization infinitely easier than with traditional opaque storage totes. Plus, the clever hinged lid opens either way for easy access.

Sources indicate that solo Stove has long been a perennial favorite for us here at Men’s Health. Its latest Basecamp fire pit combines a just-right size that’s roomy enough for four adults to enjoy yet compact enough to easily transport from the backyard to the backseat for car camping. And, of course, it still features the same smokeless design and maximum burn efficiency that the brand is known for.

Leatherman’s Signal has been my multitool of choice since I can remember. The just-right tool selection includes everything you need for a day in the backcountry or your own backyard: Pliers, drivers, cutters, a saw, a micro hammer, bottle and can openers, wrenches, and a 420 HC combo knife. Plus, there’s a whistle and ferro rod if you need ‘em. It’s all packed into one compact tool that stuffs neatly in the available sheath or clips to your pack with the brand that invented the ultra-packable camp chair sought to make it even better. With an extended backrest, it’s now more comfortable and supportive than ever, with all the same backpacking-friendly packability as before. The shock-corded pole structure makes for easy setup, and the 100% recycled polyester seat fabric is a nice, eco-friendly touch.
